Clients can replace their own access code using TIS. When clients lose or forget their access code, they are unable to access TIS or complete electronic claimant’s reports. However, it is possible for a Service Canada agent to replace the original access code or issue a temporary one. Replacing the access code with either the original code or a temporary code automatically restores the client’s access to these services.

Some antedates can be adjudicated at Level 1 according to the National Policy on Levels of Decision . The claim type (CT) affects the conditions for allowing the antedate at Level 1. If the issue is not within Level 1 authority, the agent reassigns the corresponding WI to Level 2. National Policy on Levels of Decision If the client does not qualify to establish a claim on any day between the date of the requested benefit period (BP) and the BPC, the Level 1 agent can deny the antedate request under the National Policy on Levels of Decision , whether or not the claim is established. National Policy on Levels of Decision Under the National Policy on Levels of Decision , a Level 1 officer can render the decision to deny an antedate request if the client does not qualify for benefits at any time between the client’s requested benefit period start date and the week of the established or tentative BPC. In this situation, the Level 1 officer can render the decision to deny the antedate whether or not the claim is established. National Policy on Levels of Decision

If good cause exists for only part of the period of delay, Level 2 agents may consider a partial antedate if the client shows good cause for the period immediately before the date the application for benefits was submitted. For an initial claim, the client must also be able to establish a claim for benefits at the requested date. Failing that, if the client qualifies for benefits on a date subsequent to that for which the antedate was requested, the antedate can be considered as of that subsequent date. In this situation, the client can be entitled to a partial antedate.

Some clients are considered available even if they actually are not. These include: clients who are referred to a training, program of instruction or employment activity; clients who are employed under a WS program; fishers (in certain situations). Clients who had a fishing benefit period (BP) established, whether for summer or winter fishing, are considered available for work with regard to their fishing activities. During the periods stated below, a 3 - Not available disentitlement (D3) is not imposed, for the sole reason that the client took part in fishing activities: Summer fishing: starting the week in which October 1 falls to the week in which the following June 15 falls. Winter fishing: starting the week in which April 1 falls to the week in which the following December 15 falls.

Some clients are deemed unemployed, capable of and available for work without having to prove their availability: clients who are referred to a training, a program of instruction or employment activity; clients who are employed under a work-sharing program; fishers (in certain situations). Clients who establish a fishing benefit period, whether for winter or for summer fishing, are considered available for work with regard to their fishing activities . During the periods mentioned below, a 3 - Not available (D3) disentitlement is not imposed for the sole reason that the client took part in fishing activities: Summer fishing: starting the week in which October 1 falls to the week in which the following June 15 falls. Winter fishing: starting the week in which April 1 falls to the week in which the following December 15 falls.

When a Claim Assessment (CA) or Specialized Application (SA) WI is received, the officer must complete the initial calculation of a claim. When a Claim Review (CR) WI with a recalculation issue is received, the officer must complete a new calculation of a previously finalized claim. A recalculation is sometimes referred to as a “recomp.” Once an initial calculation is successfully transmitted, a claim must be recalculated when new information is received that will have an effect on the previous calculation result (e.g. an amended ROE is issued). When a recalculation is required for an Integrity case, an urgent Action Item (AI) WI is created for the recalculation. The officer assigned to this WI must complete the recalculation. The recalculation of a claim can affect the following: the client’s ability to establish a benefit period (BP); benefit period the client’s entitlement to benefits; the client’s benefit rate. Note

Regardless of how an officer organizes the work, the officer assigned to complete the calculation of a claim must ensure that any issues are addressed and all the facts required to calculate the claim are on file before completing the calculation. Unless otherwise noted in the procedures, the officer must not complete the calculation until all related WIs necessary to finalize the calculation are completed. If the calculation cannot be completed because of an outstanding related WI, the WI for calculation is moved to Pending until the related WI is completed. Multiple officers may be assigned WIs for the same claim being assessed (e.g. one officer is assigned an ROE reason for separation [RFS] Action WI and one is assigned the CA WI). The officers complete only the WI to which they are assigned unless instructed otherwise by a procedure. When assessing the claim, the officer assigned the calculation must also review any client Note for actions required (e.g. inputting transactions, sending letters). When the calculation is complete, the officer must communicate the decision to the client as necessary.

Parents can share parental benefits. For more information and definitions, the officer can refer to Parents: Definition — Table . Parents: Definition — Table The type of parental benefits requested by the first parent to apply determines the type of parental benefits all parents are entitled to receive for the same birth, adoption or placement, regardless of which parent is paid first. When fact-finding with parents who applied for benefits after the first parent, the officer informs the other parents of this. Once at least one week of parental benefits has been paid to any parent, all parents requesting parental benefits for the same birth, adoption or placement are only entitled to receive the type of parental benefits selected by the first parent who applied for benefits. The maximum shareable entitlement is 40 weeks of standard parental benefits or 69 weeks of extended parental benefits for children born or placed for adoption on or after March 17, 2019. For children born or placed for adoption before this date, the maximum shareable entitlement is 35 weeks of standard parental benefits or 61 weeks of extended parental benefits. The maximum entitlement for one client remains at 35 weeks of standard or 61 weeks of extended benefits. Clients can change the number of weeks that each parent receives at any time before all benefits are paid. When clients cannot agree on the number of weeks they will each receive, the officer reassigns the issue to a Level 2 officer who adjudicates the division of the remaining weeks. If the client has a violation on file, the increased entrance requirements may apply. The CER applies to claims with a BPC between September 26, 2021 (w/c 2310), and September 18, 2022 (w/c 2361). During this period, the definitions for major attached and minor attached clients in the EIA 6(1) are repealed. Clients whose claims are established with 420 hours of insurable employment qualify for special benefits. The officer ensures that all other qualifying and entitlement conditions are met. increased entrance requirements

Adjudicating the last employment in the qualifying period (QP) — BPCs between w/c 2310 and w/c 2361 Budget 2021 has introduced a temporary simplification measure starting September 26, 2021. For claims with a BPC between w/c 2310 and w/c 2361, the officer will only adjudicate the last period of employment in the QP if it is contentious. If the officer allows the last RFS, all other ROEs in the QP, even if they are contentious, are used to calculate the claim. If, however, the officer does not allow the RFS on the last ROE in the QP, the claim is calculated with a disqualification. Note This new measure does not apply to self-employment (SE) and fishing claims. If clients applying for SE or fishing benefits have a BPC w/c 2310 and later, insurable employment in the QP and any contentious RFSs, these RFSs must be adjudicated following normal adjudication procedures. When the client declares other employers with a contentious RFS on the same application, if ACP does not allow the issue under auto-adjudication rules, the issue is automatically resolved and ACP creates a record of decision (ROD) that shows Adjudication not Required . The Special condition field on the ROE is not updated, and the ROE is included in the calculation. An ADJ WI is not created for the RFS. When there is more than one ROE with the same last day paid (LDP), and one of the ROEs is contentious while the other ROE is not, adjudication is not required and both ROEs will be included in the calculation. Adjudication not required: Reason for separation (RFS) beyond 12 weeks — BPCs between w/c 2258 and w/c 2309 Adjudication principles on initial claims or recalculations with a BPC between w/c 2258 and w/c 2309 only apply to the RFS on the last employment in the QP and to contentious RFS issues that fall in the 12-week period before the interruption of earnings (I of E) used to establish the claim. Adjudication not previously required — Specialized ACP process A new specialized process that streamlines the processing of initial applications was introduced on September 27, 2020. Claims processed in this specialized ACP process were established without adjudicating contentious RFS issues in the QP. The RFS issues that were not previously adjudicated can be identified because the Special condition field was left blank on the ROE but the ROE was still included in the initial calculation. Note If a contentious RFS in the QP was not adjudicated on an initial claim for regular benefits as it went through the specialized ACP process, it does not need to be adjudicated on the renewal claim, as long as the client is still requesting regular benefits. However, there may be an outstanding ADJ WI. If there is an outstanding ADJ WI for a contentious RFS in the QP, the officer does not adjudicate the issue. To remove the outstanding ADJ WI, the officer sends a request to an authorized user to delete it. If there is both a CA Renewal WI and an outstanding ADJ WI for a contentious RFS in the QP, the Level 1 officer processes the CA Renewal WI even though the ADJ WI remains outstanding. The officer: determines the effective date of the renewal; inputs the renewal and completes the registration number; completes the CA Renewal WI. The officer completes the CA Renewal WI before sending the request to an authorized user to delete the outstanding ADJ WI. Note

Foreign nationals whose post-graduation work permit expires between September 20, 2021 and December 31, 2023 can work in Canada for an additional 18 months or until the expiry of their passport, whichever comes first. Eligible post-graduation work permit holders received an email in August 2022 from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) granting them interim work authorization until May 31, 2023. These clients are considered to have maintained status for EI purposes: If the permit expired between September 20, 2021 and October 1, 2022, a proof that the client submitted an application to renew the work permit before December 31, 2022 is required. If the permit expired between October 2, 2022 and December 31, 2022 and the client had a valid passport and address on file with IRCC, no application is required and a new work permit was automatically issued to the client. If the permit expired between October 2, 2022 and December 31, 2022 and the client did not have a valid passport or valid address on file with IRCC, a proof that the client filed an application to renew the work permit is required. Eligible post-graduation work permit holders received an email in April 2023 from IRCC granting them interim work authorization until May 31, 2024. These clients are considered to have maintained status for EI purposes: If the permit expired between September 20, 2021 and December 31, 2023, proof that the client filed a registration through the simplified process (before May 21, 2023) or proof that the client filed an application between April 6, 2023 and December 31, 2023 to renew the work permit is required. Note In In order for the client to be granted maintained status, the client needs to provide the following documents: a copy of the work permit; a copy of the interim work authorization email received from IRCC; And one of the following based on the client`s situation: a proof of application for a new work permit or a renewal; a proof of registration through the simplified process; a statement from the client that the client was not required to submit an application (i.e. the client had a valid passport and address); a new work permit. If a client’s work permit expires before the receipt of the email from IRCC, the client must provide proof of an authorization to remain in Canada by means of a visitor’s permit, a study permit or another work permit.

Up until June 30, 2013, it was possible to extend the BP for all weeks where the disentitlement prevented the client from receiving EI benefits. A claim can be active, terminated, blocked or archived. The CS impacts which transactions can be input and when the letter of decision is sent: Active: The active claim is established and is currently displayed automatically in FTS. It is a claim for which benefits are still payable and that has not been terminated. Terminated: A terminated claim is showing on the Dormant tab in FTS. It has ended but can be reactivated. Once the transaction to reactivate the claim has been processed, all inputs for the claim must be done the same way as an active claim. Blocked: In some cases, the claim that the officer must reconsider is on the Dormant tab in FTS, but there is a new active claim established and displayed on the Summary screen. The officer makes adjustments to this type of claim using BCS if the blocked status shows 1 - Updateable . Otherwise, IPOC intervention is required. Archived: Claims that are more than 7 years old are moved from the Dormant tab to the Archived tab. The officer can view an archived claim by changing the status of the archived claim from 1 - Non-Viewable to 2 - Viewable in FTS. Once the officer requests to make the claim viewable, the status field immediately displays 2 - Viewable and the claim becomes viewable the next business day for 2 weeks. Adjustments to this type of claim are processed with IPOC intervention.

Once the transaction to reactivate the claim has been processed, all inputs for the claim must be done the same as for an active claim. Blocked: In some cases, the claim that the officer must reconsider is on the Dormant tab in FTS, but there is a new active claim established and displayed on the Summary screen. The officer makes adjustments to this type of claim using BCS if the blocked CS shows 1 - Updateable . Otherwise, IPOC intervention is required. Archived: Claims that are more than 7 years old are moved from the Dormant tab to the Archived tab. The officer can view an archived claim by changing the status of the archived claim from 1 - Non-Viewable to 2 - Viewable in FTS. Once the officer requests to make the claim viewable, the status field immediately displays 2 - Viewable and the claim becomes viewable the next business day for 2 weeks. Adjustments to this type of claim are processed with IPOC intervention. Determining the order of FTS inputs Controlled, multiple-day inputs in FTS are required to establish separate OPs for each decision (e.g. unreported earnings and reason for separation (RFS)). When there is more than one reconsideration decision that results in an OP, the decisions must be input in the following order: Callout Controlled inputs in FTS are also required for UP and OP situations. The officer processes the inputs resulting in the OP first. Once the OP is established, the officer inputs an agreed deduction equal to the benefit rate amount. They are farm or horticulture employees who work at least 5 days and 35 hours per week. They are employees who receive lay days or periods of leave because they regularly work more than normally worked by those employed full-time elsewhere. Clients can change the type of parental benefits requested if the request is made before any parental benefits have been paid to any parent. Once at least one week of parental benefits has been paid to any parent (even as little as $1), the type of parental benefits that was selected by the first parent who applied cannot be changed . If any other parent is paid a different type of parental benefits than the type selected by the first parent who applied, the benefit type (BT) on the other parents’ claims is converted to the BT selected by the first parent. If a request to change the type of parental benefits is submitted before benefits have been paid, although benefits are subsequently paid as a result of processing delays or automated payments, the request may still be granted.

A transitional measure under which ACP automatically adjudicated and allowed all training effective September 27, 2020 has ended on September 11, 2021. The intent of this measure was to prevent any delay in payment to clients who reported training. For regular benefits, clients must still be able to prove that they are capable of and available for work while attending non-referred training. Service Canada has the authority to impose a retroactive 3 - Not available disentitlement (D3) if the client is unable to prove availability, even if ACP initially allowed the training. Therefore, if the client reports not being available while attending non-referred training, and benefits were previously paid for this period, the officer reviews the client’s availability. When the Level 2 officer determines that the client has not proven availability from the start date of the course, the officer imposes a retroactive D3. The officer refers to BE 2020-05 — Emergency Response Benefit Transition Provisions , Digest 10.3 — Credibility and 10.12 — Courses of instruction/employment measures for more information on availability. BE 2020-05 — Emergency Response Benefit Transition Provisions 10.3 — Credibility 10.12 — Courses of instruction/employment measures For special benefits, the client must still meet the entitlement conditions for the requested benefit type (BT) while attending non-referred training. A client attending non-referred training may provide information on a claimant’s report or during a conversation with an officer that brings into question the entitlement to special benefits. In this case, the officer creates a WI for the training issue and follows normal adjudication procedures, even if ACP initially allowed the training.

Note The benefit period (BP) can be extended to a maximum of 104 weeks to pay additional weeks of special benefits when the client did not receive the maximum entitlement during the initial BP. BPs for QPIP clients and self-employment (SE) clients can also be extended under these circumstances. special benefits The system automatically extends the BP (and parental window [PW] if applicable) for each type of special benefits where at least one week (or one equivalent week in the case of QPIP benefits) was paid in the initial BP. This extension is generated when the system processes the claimant’s report for the last renewable week and when all the following conditions are met: no regular benefits were paid in the initial BP; more than one type of special benefits was paid (or equivalent in the case of QPIP benefits); fewer weeks than the maximum entitlement was paid for at least one of these special benefits; the maximum number of combined special benefits to which the client is entitled is greater than 50 weeks. If a specific type of special benefits was not paid during the initial BP, it cannot be paid during the extended BP. Client’s address Clients must provide their permanent address in their EI application. If clients have been temporarily displaced because of the flooding, they can also provide their temporary address. This temporary mailing address can be a hotel, a community centre, etc. Mail delivery If clients need more information about mail delivery, they can refer to the Canada Post website or call 1-888-550-6333. Canada Post website Interim ROEs Since employers may not be able to issue ROEs, the officer must create an interim ROE as soon as possible for clients affected by the flooding. Direct deposit Clients may need to update their direct deposit information. When in contact with client, the officer must always make sure the direct deposit information on file is correct. Payment replacement If a client affected by the flooding requests a replacement payment for an outstanding cheque, the officer can issue the payment replacement immediately. For instructions, the officer refers to Processing a warrant replacement request submitted by a client procedure . Clients are major attached when they have accumulated at least 600 hours of insurable employment during their qualifying period (QP). The CT is 3 - Sickness - major attached . Clients are minor attached when they have accumulated between 420 and 599 hours of insurable employment during their QP. Minor attached clients have the required number of hours to establish a claim for regular benefits but they do not have the required 600 hours for sickness benefits. Minor attached clients are entitled to sickness benefits only if the reason for separation (RFS) is other than illness. In these cases, the CT is 9 - Sickness - minor attached . Defining major and minor attached clients — Common entrance requirement (from w/c 2310 to w/c 2361) As part of Budget 2021, the Government of Canada announced that a national common entrance requirement of 420 hours of insurable employment is required to establish a claim for regular or special benefits. If the client has a violation on file, increased entrance requirements may apply. The common entrance requirement applies to claims with a BPC between September 26, 2021 (w/c 2310) and September 18, 2022 (w/c 2361). During this period, the definitions for major attachment claimant and minor attachment claimant in EIA 6(1) are repealed. All claims established with 420 hours of insurable employment qualify for special benefits. increased entrance requirements

A temporary measure to waive the one-week WP has been implemented to support clients impacted by major changes in economic conditions due to the imposition of tariffs by the United States. The WP is waived for all initial claims with a BPC between March 30, 2025 (w/c 2493) and October 10 , 2026 (w/c 2572 ), regardless of the requested benefit type (BT). If it is advantageous to the client, the client can decide to serve the WP (e.g. the client must serve the WP to receive supplemental unemployment benefits [SUB]). The WP waiver is automatically applied to all claims except claims for special benefits in which there is a SUB code. The officer must verify and enter the appropriate SUB code if the client is receiving SUB . When recalculating a claim and the only change is adding or removing a SUB plan from the ROE, the calculation result will indicate NCA - No changes to the claim . In this situation, the officer manually enters or removes the WP waiver. A client who applies, qualifies for and is payable benefits before March 30, 2025 (w/c 2493) cannot request to postdate the start date of their claim solely to benefit from this temporary measure. A client may request to have their claim start in the week they applied for benefits when both of the following conditions are met: The client applied for benefits on or after March 30, 2025 (w/c 2493). The Administrative Policy was applied and resulted in a BPC before March 30, 2025 (w/c 2493). For more information, the officer refers to Determining the client’s entitlement to the waived waiting period due to Pilot Project No. 24: Measures to respond to major changes in economic conditions . When a claim is renewed with less than 5 weeks remaining to be paid, the renewal application can be used to establish a subsequent initial claim. Clients are advised at the time of the renewal that if they work between the date of the renewal application and the date the renewed claim terminates they must complete a new EI application. For client service purposes however, the officer can use the original renewal application to set-up the subsequent claim if the client can provide the specific details of the employment between the renewal date and the start date of the subsequent claim. An interim ROE can be used, but the officer must also advise the client to provide an ROE. An EI application received immediately following the end of a previous claim (e.g. no entitlement is left or the claim end week has been reached) is also considered a subsequent initial claim. The procedure used to determine the BPC of a subsequent claim is different from the procedure used for an initial claim. BPC

When a claim is renewed with less than 5 weeks remaining to be paid, the renewal application can be used to establish a subsequent initial claim. Clients are advised at the time of the renewal that if they work between the date of the renewal application and the date the renewed claim terminates, they must complete a new EI application. For client service purposes however, the officer can use the original renewal application to set up the subsequent claim if the client can provide the specific details of the employment between the renewal date and the start date of the subsequent claim. An interim ROE can be used, but the officer must also advise the client to provide an ROE. An EI application received immediately following the end of a previous claim (e.g. no entitlement is left or the claim end week has been reached) is also considered a subsequent initial claim. The procedure used to determine the BPC of a subsequent claim is different from the procedure used for an initial claim. determine the BPC When establishing a subsequent claim, the officer verifies the number of entitlement weeks received from the previous claim in order to determine how many payable weeks remain in the benefit period (BP). Doing this avoids creating an overpayment (OP). If necessary, the officer updates the Caregiver/Compassionate care data entry (MCB1) screen and adjusts the amount of entitlement weeks requested on the subsequent claim on the Caregiver/Compassionate care entitlement (M112) screen. The officer refers to the CCB and family caregiver benefits: Claim set-up or amendment — Input guide for input guidance. CCB and family caregiver benefits: Claim set-up or amendment — Input guide

When a claim is converted to MPS or sent to purge and recreate (P/R) for manual adjustment, the year-to-date tax amounts are transferred from the CPS tax file to the MPS tax file with a system generated T070-3 transaction. Recreating the claim prematurely causes a tax error.

In FTS, claims that are more than 7 years old are moved from the Dormant tab to the Archived tab. The default status of an archived claim is 1 - Non-viewable . In some situations (e.g. during an ongoing litigation), a retention hold indicator is imposed on an archived claim to retain the claim in FTS for as long as it is required. These archived claims are displayed with a 3 - Non-viewable - Retain or 4 - Viewable - Retain status. The IPOC officer selects the appropriate status in the drop-down menu of the Update Status column on the Archived tab to change the status of an archived claim from 1 - Non-viewable to 2 - Viewable . The status field displays 2 - Viewable immediately and the requested claim becomes viewable the next business day. The status automatically changes back to 1 - Non-viewable after approximately 2 weeks. The IPOC officer can change the status of multiple BPCs to 2 - Viewable or 4 - Viewable - Retain for the same SIN. All requests to dearchive claims are recorded in the Transaction History screen as an ARC01 - Archive - Status change transaction. The record of the transaction includes the BPC and the change in archived claim status.

The amount payable to the client is calculated by dividing the number of hours missed due to WS by the number of NWH on the claim and multiplying the result by the EI benefit rate. Amount payable to the client = Hours missed due to WS ÷ NWH x EI benefit rate. Example: 4.5 (hours missed due to WS) ÷ 40 (NWH) = .1125 x $425 (EI benefit rate) = 47.8125. The client is payable $48. The IPOC officer uses 4 decimal points on the calculator and round off appropriately. If not, the sum would be $47. If there are earnings from non-WS employment, the amount is reduced according to the normal allowable rules.

Parents can share parental benefits. For more information and definitions, the officer refers to Parents: Definition — Table . Parents: Definition — Table The type of parental benefits requested by the first parent to apply determines the type of parental benefits all parents are entitled to receive for that same birth, adoption or placement, regardless of which parent is paid first. When fact-finding with parents who applied for benefits after the first parent, the officer informs the other parents of this. Once at least one week of parental benefits has been paid to any parent, all parents requesting parental benefits for the same birth, adoption or placement are only entitled to the type of parental benefits selected by the first parent who applied for benefits. The maximum shareable entitlement is 40 weeks of standard parental benefits or 69 weeks of extended parental benefits for children born or placed for adoption on or after March 17, 2019. For children born or placed for adoption before this date, the maximum shareable entitlement is 35 weeks of standard parental benefits or 61 weeks of extended parental benefits. The maximum entitlement for one client remains at 35 weeks of standard or 61 weeks of extended benefits. Clients can change the number of weeks that each parent receives at any time before all benefits are paid. When clients cannot agree on the number of weeks they will each receive, the officer completes the CR Parental Benefits Validation WI and creates an Action Item (AI) WI to refer the issue to a Level 2 officer for adjudication on the division of the remaining weeks.

A triage process was developed to convert URs received through the Data Gateway and upload them to FTS. Since the triage process cannot action UR declarations with comments, a workaround was created to notify an IPOC officer to review all UR declarations with comments. The triage process converts the UR and inputs special condition code 11 - Non-available and sick days are greater than 5 in all declarations that contain a comment. IPOC officers need to familiarize themselves with this workaround because there are 2 scenarios where declarations can be coded with special condition code 11 . The 2 scenarios are: An IPOC officer inputs special condition code 11 to reject a UR declaration if not available days and sick days are greater than 5. NWS generates an IPOC System Notification (IPOC SN) Work-sharing - Special condition WI. The rejected client record is also available for review on the WD0242 EDS report. The triage process inputs special condition code 11 to reject a UR declaration with a comment. The SIN is added to an .XML file in the Rejected_Declarations subfolder. The IPOC officer reviews all other information on the UR to determine the correct action to take to address the special condition code.

Fraudulent paper ROEs were created without the knowledge of the true SIN-holder and the employer associated with the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) BN indicated in block 5 of the ROE. There are also instances where there are reasons to suspect that the business identified on the ROE is illegitimate or suspicious and was created to issue fraudulent ROEs. These fraudulent ROEs were sent to Service Canada and scanned as documents in support of fraudulent applications for benefits, or uploaded in AW or MSCA. A close examination may reveal a difference in the font and size of the characters in the serial number of these ROEs when compared to the normal format. In some cases, RCM validates the serial number and does not signal the ROE as a duplicate, because that serial number was used to establish an EI claim more than 11 years ago. In other situations, the serial number has been issued within the last 11 years to a different BN than the one used on the fraudulent ROE, however, RCM validates the serial number but does not flag it as a duplicate because the ROE was never used to establish an EI claim. When reviewing a claim, the officer may realize that an ROE assigned to a client is fraudulent. Fraudulent ROEs can be identified at any stage of the claim assessment process, or while conducting fact-finding with the client whose application is being assessed. Fraud can also be identified at the call centre or at the Service Canada Centre (SCC), if clients report receiving an ROE in MSCA that does not belong to them. The officer deletes the ROE in RCM, suspends the application process, if necessary, and refers the file to Integrity, if the file is not already under investigation. For more information, officers refer to Fraud indicators: Identifying potentially fraudulent claims — Knowledge . Fraud indicators: Identifying potentially fraudulent claims — Knowledge

When a client stops working for an employer due to illness, injury or quarantine, the officer must verify FTS and determine if the employer is enrolled in the EI PRP. Employers enrolled in the PRP have been granted a reduction of their EI premiums payable because they have demonstrated that they provide their employees a specific amount of PSL or WLI benefits that meets the standards of the PRP. The details of the specific benefits provided by the employer are available in FTS. Many employers have multiple business numbers. Whenever possible, it is important to search for the employer using the business number indicated on the ROE, as not all business numbers have the same entitlement to employee benefits. Note If the client is not entitled to the benefits as shown in the details of the plan, the officer fact-finds with the employer to determine why the client is not entitled to the benefits.

An employer may provide a period of PSL to an employee who is unable to work due to illness, injury or quarantine. An employee’s entitlement to PSL may be based on a predetermined amount of paid sick time allowed by the employer each year, or it may be based on a formula related to an employee’s years of service. The employer can even advance future sick leave entitlements to an employee who does not have enough entitlement to cover the entire period of leave. PSL is considered benefits that might otherwise be paid by EI. Clients who are entitled to PSL and who stop working due to illness or injury must exhaust their sick leave credits before they are eligible to receive EI sickness benefits. If a client is entitled to PSL and does not apply to use it, the sick leave entitlement is still deemed earnings and is allocated to the period for which the entitlement would have been paid or payable if the client had requested the paid leave from the employer. Preventive withdrawal payments may be paid to an employee who stops working because the working conditions present physical danger to the employee’s health, danger to an unborn child or to a child the employee is breast-feeding. Preventive withdrawal payments are paid under provincial legislation and are currently only available in the province of Quebec. An EI claim must be on file to input direct deposit information. The claim does not have to be active. If there is no claim on file, the officer refers to Adding a direct deposit — No claim on file . Adding a direct deposit — No claim on file If there is already direct deposit information on the claim, the officer refers to Modifying a direct deposit . Modifying a direct deposit Direct deposit payments can only be made to financial institutions located in Canada. Interstate or commuter clients who file a claim against Canada are also eligible for direct deposit payments, if the financial institution is in Canada. Direct deposit payments must be made to a financial account that accepts deposits (i.e. a chequing or savings account). The account must be in the client’s name, or if it is a joint account, the client must be one of the account holders. Direct deposit payments must not be made to third party accounts, except in cases involving appointment of representatives. If a designated representative is registered on the claim, only this representative can request direct deposit changes because the client is no longer authorized to do so. For more information, the officer refers to Appointment of representative — Limited physical or mental capacity . Appointment of representative — Limited physical or mental capacity Note Note Clients can provide direct deposit information either by telephone, MSCA or by filling out the Direct Deposit: INS5178 — Application Form . If they complete the INS5178 form, they can either fill in their banking information or provide a void cheque. Direct Deposit: INS5178 — Application Form Note

On November 1, 2021, changes were made to EI systems to prevent updating an EI ERB claim when all the following conditions are met: The $2 000 advance payment has been issued. The update affects the 65 - Lump Sum Payment ($2000) - Canadian Emergency Response code (D65) on file. The lump sum payment modification code is: Blank B - Added SIN Change N - $1500 established as overpayment P - $1000 established as overpayment Q - $500 established as overpayment This system change was required to start the reconciliation process of the advance payment and establish an overpayment (OP) if clients did not serve the 4 full weeks of the D65. This process ended in July 2022. When adjusting an EI ERB claim manually, the IPOC officer only establishes a portion of the $2 000 advance payment as an OP for weeks of served D65 that now become non-payable due to an overlapping new decision. The IPOC officer establishes an OP for each week with a D65 that becomes non-payable and adjusts the pay history summary (PHS) as required. When establishing an OP for the $2 000 advance payment, the IPOC officer selects the contract object type ERB2 - CERB Advance Payment in PSCD and the OP message code 46 - You are no longer entitled to the advanced payment of Canada Emergency Response Benefits you have received. This caused an overpayment . For more information on establishing a debt in PSCD, the IPOC officer refers to Creating a debt in PSCD . Creating a debt in PSCD When an OP has been established for a portion or all of the $2 000 advance payment, in FTS, the IPOC officer updates the Lump sum payment modification field of the Emergency Response Benefits screen to code D, N, P or Q as follows: If the full $2 000 advance payment has been established as an OP, the IPOC officer selects D - Established as overpayment . If $1 500 from the advance payment has been established as an OP, the IPOC officer selects N - $1500 established as overpayment . On November 1, 2021, changes were made to EI systems to prevent updating an EI ERB claim when all of the following conditions are met: The $2 000 advance payment has been issued. The update affects the 65 - Lump Sum Payment ($2000) - Canadian Emergency Response code (D65) on file. The lump sum payment modification code is: Blank B - Added SIN Change N - $1500 established as overpayment P - $1000 established as overpayment Q - $500 established as overpayment This system change was required to start the reconciliation process of the advance payment and establish an overpayment (OP) if clients did not serve the 4 full weeks of the D65. This process ended in July 2022. When the officer inputs a transaction on an updateable EI ERB claim in BCS, a B112 error code may be displayed if the lump sum modification code on the Emergency Response Benefits screen is blank, B, N, P or Q and that transaction affects the $2 000 advance payment. When the claim cannot be updated in BCS due to error code B112, the IPOC officer establishes an OP for the full $2 000 advance payment if the lump sum payment modification code on the Emergency Response Benefits screen is blank or B. If the lump sum payment modification code on the Emergency Response Benefits screen is N, P or Q, the system has established an OP for a portion of the $2 000 advance payment. The IPOC officer establishes an OP for the outstanding balance. When establishing an OP for the $2 000 advance payment, the IPOC officer selects the contract object type ERB2 - CERB Advance Payment in PSCD and the OP message code 46 - You are no longer entitled to the advanced payment of Canada Emergency Response Benefits you have received. This caused an overpayment . For more information on establishing a debt in PSCD, the IPOC officer refers to Creating a debt in PSCD . Then, the IPOC officer updates the Lump sum payment modification field of the Emergency Response Benefits screen to D - Established as overpayment and re-inputs transactions in BCS. BCS performs an administrative reconciliation of the advance payment OP by rescinding and recouping served D65 on the client’s file. Clients initially received the full amount of the EI ERB even if they reported income . However, clients were not paid if they reported a full work week (FWW) or finding full-time employment on a Sunday or Monday, which resulted in a found work code being imposed. When reviewing income on an EI ERB claim, the officer reviews the 2-week periods separately starting from the first week that the EI ERB was paid. The officer confirms that the eligibility requirements have been met under EIA 153.9 (1)(a)(iv) and (v) that is the client stopped working and had no income for at least 7 consecutive days in the 2-week period being reviewed. If the client has not had a period of 7 consecutive days of no work and no income, the officer applies EIA 153. 9(4) to determine if the income exceeds $1 000 over a 4-week period. Monies are considered income if both of the following conditions are met: The monies arise from employment. The monies were earned during the period for which the EI ERB is paid. Separation monies and monies paid for work that took place before or after the period for which the EI ERB is paid are not considered income. In order to review the client’s eligibility for the EI ERB paid, the officer conducts a fact-finding about the nature, origin and purpose of the monies received. The officer considers the following factors: Does the payment arise out of employment? When were the monies earned? Is it during the EI ERB period or during an earlier or later period of work? Who is making the payment? Is it someone other than the employer? What is the reason for the payment? When a client with a 900-series SIN submits a work permit, the officer reviews it to determine the type of work permit and if there are any restrictions. The officer assesses the availability of a client who holds a valid work permit based on the individual circumstances, taking into consideration all the terms of the work permit. When a client indicates availability for work, and there is no issue with the work permit or any contradictory evidence on file concerning the client’s availability, the officer determines the client’s entitlement to benefits as for any other client. Open work permit Foreign workers with open work permits are allowed to accept employment from any employer they choose for the length of time shown on the work permit. Non-renewable work permit Foreign workers with non-renewable work permits cannot renew their work permit and the duration of their stay in Canada cannot be extended beyond the work permit’s expiration date. This type of work permit is generally issued to workers in the Seasonal Agricultural Program but may also be applicable to other streams. These clients receive a work permit that is valid for a specific period, which normally corresponds with the type of work permit issued. Once the permit expires, the client must leave Canada. Employer-specific work permit Foreign workers whose work permit includes a restriction that only allows them to work for a specific employer are not normally considered to be available to accept work from other employers and may be disentitled from receiving benefits. However, the work permit restriction is not the only factor to consider when determining availability. For example, the client may be able to have the work permit amended once employment is obtained. The officer considers all factors that are normally taken into account when determining the client’s availability. The client must: be available and actively seeking work with other employers; reasonably expect that IRCC will remove this restriction from the work permit once new employment is found; be advised to apply to IRCC for a new work permit or to have the restriction removed from the work permit once new employment is found; be advised to inform Service Canada if IRCC denies the renewal application. Pending a decision from IRCC, foreign workers who apply to have a restriction removed from their work permit continue to be entitled to benefits, provided they prove their availability. If IRCC denies the client’s application for a new work permit, or the request to have a restriction removed from an existing work permit, the client is no longer able to demonstrate availability for work, and the officer imposes a disentitlement from the date the decision was made by IRCC. If there are doubts about the client’s availability for a reason that is not related to the work permit, the officer refers to Availability for further information. Availability

BCS allows certain types of transactions to be processed on blocked dormant claims. There are 2 options available: Estimate and Claim update . Updating a blocked claim When transactions must be input on a blocked claim, the officer reviews the Blocked tab in FTS to determine the BCS status. If the status of the claim is 1 - Updateable , the officer requests an update using BCS and processes the transactions. Note An update in BCS can only be done on one BPC at a time. When transactions are input but not processed, Yes appears in the Block Action Pending column and access is denied for input on all other BPCs until the requested transactions are processed. Access to a BPC with a pending action is limited to the officer who initiated that action. If an update is requested by the officer but cannot be completed by BCS, on the next processing day, the “Blocked claim not updated or not calculated” message is displayed along with the exception, error or warning on the MR05 screen. officers review the exception, error or warning on the Results tab in BCS for further action. If the update cannot be completed using BCS, the system presents an estimate result. The decision can be sent to IPOC using the Forward via MM06 link which creates the prefilled the Renewal/Revised (M106) and MM06 transactions. Estimate function The Estimate function in BCS allows officers to view and evaluate the end results without processing the transactions. Estimates are possible for blocked claims with a 1 - Updateable status as well as unblocked dormant claims, provided the CS is 05 (inactive) or 06 (terminated) . BCS Estimate transactions are processed overnight and the results are available on the Results tab the next day. officers that have requested an estimate can view the end result and forward the request for IPOC intervention using the prefilled MM06 available on the Results tab.

BCS allows certain types of transactions to be processed on blocked dormant claims. There are 2 options available: Estimate and Claim update . Claim update function When transactions must be input on a blocked claim, the Blocked Claims System tab in FTS must be reviewed to determine the CS in BCS. If the CS is 1 - Updateable , an update is requested using BCS and the transactions can be processed. Note An update in BCS can only be done on one BPC at a time. When transactions are input but not processed, Yes appears in the Block Action Pending column and access is denied for input on all other BPCs until the requested transactions are processed. Access to a BPC with a pending action is limited to the agent who initiated that action. If an update is requested by the agent but cannot be completed by BCS, on the next processing day, the “Blocked claim not updated or not calculated” message is displayed along with the exception, error or warning on the MR05 screen. Agents review the exception, error or warning on the Results tab in BCS for further action. If the update cannot be completed using BCS, the system presents an estimate result. The decision can be sent to IPOC using the Forward via MM06 link, which creates the prefilled M106 and MM06. After conducting a full review of the investigation, if the Level 2 officer determines that facts are missing, the officer must return the investigation to the investigator for further fact-finding and indicate the information that is missing but necessary to adjudicate the issue. The Level 2 officer must not adjudicate the issue if facts are missing or incomplete. Facts are not considered missing or incomplete if the investigator has followed up with the client when the client fails to report for an interview or fails to reply to a request for information. The investigator is not required to send a follow-up letter but must make 2 attempts on 2 different days to contact the client by telephone. If the investigator leaves a message on a voicemail, only one attempt is required and they must allow 48 hours for the client to respond. If the investigator recommends that the Integrity case be considered as voluntary disclosure, but the investigation type is not 70 in NIIS, the officer returns the file to Integrity. The Integrity Services Branch does not verify the employer’s or third party’s version against the client’s version in the following situations: The investigation results in an actual or potential OP of less than the Integrity investigative threshold. There is no other active investigation. In these situations, the officer does not return the case to Integrity because the employer’s or the third party’s version is missing. The officer is not required to validate the threshold.

Whether or not they claim to be available for work, claimants are not entitled to receive benefits for any period during which they are an “inmate of a prison or similar institution”. Disentitlements for being an “inmate of a prison or similar institution” include pre-trial and post-trial custody as well as the following situations: incarceration by court order in order to undergo treatment, authorized absence from a detention centre or prison either to undergo treatment at another facility or to undergo an evaluation at another facility. Sickness benefits When reviewing an incarceration issue for a client requesting sickness benefits, the agent must determine whether the client is an inmate in a penal or similar institution, not whether the client is otherwise available. Clients are not entitled to sickness benefits for any period of time they are incarcerated in a prison or similar institution. Maternity benefits When reviewing an incarceration issue for a client requesting maternity benefits, the agent must determine whether the client is an inmate in a penal or similar institution, not whether the client meets the entitlement conditions for maternity benefits. Clients are not entitled to maternity benefits for any period of time they are incarcerated in a prison or similar institution. Parental benefits Entitlement to parental benefits is based on the premise that the individual making the claim provides care to a child. Incarcerated clients cannot demonstrate that they are providing care to a child. Family caregiver benefits Entitlement to family caregiver benefits is based on the premise that the individual making the claim provides care or support to a critically ill patient. Incarcerated clients cannot demonstrate that they are providing care or support to a critically ill patient. CCB Entitlement to CCB is based on the premise that the individual making the claim provides care or support to a critically ill family member. Incarcerated clients cannot demonstrate that they are providing care or support to a critically ill family member. In these situations, the agent imposes a 12 - Inmate of penal institution disentitlement (D12) for the entire period of the client’s incarceration.

Clients are not entitled to receive benefits for any period during which they are an “inmate of a prison or similar institution”. Disentitlements for being an “inmate of a prison or similar institution” include pre-trial and post-trial custody as well as the following situations: incarceration by court order in order to undergo treatment, authorized absence from a detention centre or prison either to undergo treatment at another facility or to undergo an evaluation at another facility. Sickness benefits When reviewing an incarceration issue for a client requesting sickness benefits, the agent must determine whether the client is an inmate in a penal or similar institution, not whether the client is otherwise available. Clients are not entitled to sickness benefits for any period of time they are incarcerated in a prison or similar institution. Maternity benefits When reviewing an incarceration issue for a client requesting maternity benefits, the agent must determine whether the client is an inmate in a penal or similar institution, not whether the client meets the entitlement conditions for maternity benefits. Clients are not entitled to maternity benefits for any period of time they are incarcerated in a prison or similar institution. Parental benefits Entitlement to parental benefits is based on the premise that the individual making the claim provides care to a child. Incarcerated clients cannot demonstrate that they are providing care to a child. Incarcerated clients cannot demonstrate that they are providing care or support to a critically ill patient. The National Policy on Voluntary Disclosure encourages clients, employers and third parties to come forward and voluntarily disclose misrepresentations. According to this policy, voluntary disclosure occurs when a person admits to having knowingly made a false statement. National Policy on Voluntary Disclosure An investigator may recommend that the file be reconsidered in light of the National Policy on Voluntary Disclosure . National Policy on Voluntary Disclosure There are 2 essential conditions for allowing the voluntary disclosure: There is no investigation under way in relation to the voluntary disclosure when a client admits to making a false statement. The false statement would have resulted in punitive measures such as a penalty, a warning or prosecution had there been no voluntary disclosure. According to the National Policy on Voluntary Disclosure , there is no limit to the number of times that a client can voluntarily disclose misrepresentations. National Policy on Voluntary Disclosure

Additionally, if it is determined that a disentitlement applies from the start date of the training course, the Level 2 agent imposes a retroactive D3.

Care is defined as: all care that is required because of a critically ill or injured patient’s state of health, other than the care provided by a health care professional. Support is defined as: all psychological or emotional support that is required because of a critically ill patient’s state of health. The definition of care or support can also include situations where the client spends time each day with the critically ill patient in the home, a hospice or a medical facility. An individual claiming this benefit type may require a short break from providing care or support for the critically ill patient. That is why benefits are not automatically denied when the client stops providing care for only a few days. The agent determines whether the client continues to be entitled to benefits based on the merits of each individual case. If it becomes apparent that the client is not providing care or support based on the definitions above, the client is disentitled from benefits. For more information, the agent can refer to Digest 22.2.4 — Care or support of critically ill or injured child or adult . Digest 22.2.4 — Care or support of critically ill or injured child or adult

Many employers have developed work patterns in which employees work excessive hours in a work week and are compensated for the excessive hours with a period of leave. Common examples of these work patterns are: 2 and 1: 12 hours per day, 7 days per week for 2 weeks followed by one week off; 3 and 1: 10 hours per day, 7 days per week for 3 weeks followed by one week off. In these situations, employers normally have employees on varying rotational patterns to ensure that work continues during periods of leave for employees. Determining if a pattern of excessive hours followed by a period of leave exists does not depend on the formal contractual relationship between an employer and employee. The pattern does not have to be established on a regular and weekly basis but there should be an element of predictable repetition. The fact that the work pattern is in place is sufficient to proceed with determining if the client is not unemployed.

Common examples of these work patterns are: 2 and 1: 12 hours per day, 7 days per week for 2 weeks followed by one week off; 3 and 1: 10 hours per day, 7 days per week for 3 weeks followed by one week off. In these situations, employers normally have employees on varying rotational patterns to ensure that work continues during periods of leave for employees. Determining if a pattern of additional hours followed by a period of leave exists does not depend on the formal contractual relationship between an employer and employee. The pattern does not have to be established on a regular and weekly basis but there should be an element of predictable repetition. The fact that the work pattern is in place is sufficient to proceed with determining if the client is not unemployed.

Summary: An administrative penalty (monetary or warning letter) must be imposed if an employer makes a misrepresentation for which neither the voluntary disclosure policy nor prosecution is applicable.

Summary: An administrative penalty (monetary or warning letter) must be imposed if a client or a third party acting on behalf of the client makes a misrepresentation for which neither the voluntary disclosure policy nor prosecution is applicable.

A penalty, warning letter or a prosecution are all sanctions. A violation is an additional sanction that can be imposed on an insured individual. For the purpose of adjudicating misrepresentation, the definition of an employer is an individual employer, a corporation or an individual director, officer or agent of a corporation. For the purpose of adjudicating employer misrepresentation, an insured person is one who was employed or was previously employed in insurable employment at the time the misrepresentation was made.

A penalty, warning letter or a prosecution are all sanctions. A violation is an additional sanction that may be imposed on an insured person. For the purpose of adjudicating misrepresentation, an insured person is one who was employed or was previously employed in insurable employment at the time the misrepresentation was made.

A violation does not impact the claim being adjudicated, but it means that the insured person may need more insurable hours to qualify on future claims. A classified violation affects the client’s entrance requirements for the earlier of the following dates: the next 260 weeks; the next 2 established claims. EI ERB claims are not considered established EI claims that allow the client to gain relief from increased entrance requirements. Even if 2 BPs were established with the increased number of insurable hours required since the first notice of violation was issued, a new violation is classified as a subsequent violation if it occurs within the 260 weeks after the date the first violation was issued. Determining the increased entrance requirements Clients are subject to increased entrance requirements if they accumulate one or more classified violations in the 260 weeks before establishing an initial claim for benefits. There are no exceptions to the increased entrance requirement sanction for clients applying for special benefits. An unclassified violation does not impact the entrance requirements on subsequent claims unless it is followed by a classified violation (which would be deemed a subsequent violation). Impact of a violation on claims established with the common entrance requirement (from w/c 2310 to w/c 2361) A temporary Budget 2021 measure applies to claims with a BPC between September 26, 2021 (w/c 2310) and September 18, 2022 (w/c 2361). Based on the common entrance requirement, a client needs 420 hours of insurable employment in the qualifying period (QP) to qualify for regular and special benefits, unless there is a violation on file. When a violation is on file, the increased entrance requirements for regular and special benefits are as follows, regardless of the regional rate of unemployment (RRU): 1 - Minor violation = 525 hours 2 - Serious violation = 630 hours 3 - Very serious violation = 735 hours 4 - Subsequent violation = 840 hours

A new specialized process that streamlines the processing of initial applications was introduced on September 27, 2020. Claims processed in this specialized ACP process were established without adjudicating contentious RFS issues in the QP. The RFS issues that were not previously adjudicated can be identified because block Special condition was left blank on the ROE but the ROE was still included in the initial calculation. Note If a contentious RFS in the QP was not adjudicated on an initial claim for regular benefits as it went through the specialized ACP process, it does not need to be adjudicated on the renewal claim, as long as the client is still requesting regular benefits. However, there may be an outstanding ADJ WI. If there is an outstanding ADJ WI for a contentious RFS in the QP, the officer does not adjudicate the issue. To remove the outstanding ADJ WI, the officer sends a request to an authorized user to delete it. If there is both a CA Renewal WI and an outstanding ADJ WI for a contentious RFS in the QP, the Level 1 officer processes the CA Renewal WI even though the ADJ WI remains outstanding. The officer: determines the effective date of the renewal; inputs the renewal and completes the registration number; completes the CA Renewal WI. The officer completes the CA Renewal WI before sending the request to an authorized user to delete the outstanding ADJ WI. Note

Adjudicating the last employment in the qualifying period (QP) — BPCs between w/c 2310 and w/c 2361 Budget 2021 has introduced a temporary simplification measure starting September 26, 2021. For claims with a BPC between w/c 2310 and w/c 2361, the officer will only adjudicate the last period of employment in the QP if it is contentious. If the officer allows the last RFS, all other ROEs in the QP, even if they are contentious, are used to calculate the claim. If, however, the officer does not allow the RFS on the last ROE in the QP, the claim is calculated with a disqualification. Note This new measure does not apply to fishing claims and claims for self-employed people. Instead, if clients have insurable employment in the QP with a contentious RFS and a BPC between w/c 2310 and w/c 2361 when they apply for self-employment (SE) or fishing benefits, the officer must adjudicate the contentious RFS following normal adjudication procedures. When the client declares other employers with a contentious RFS on the same application, if ACP does not allow the issue under auto-adjudication rules, the issue is automatically resolved, and ACP creates a record of decision (ROD) that shows Adjudication not Required . Block Special condition on the ROE is not updated, and the ROE is included in the calculation. An Adjudication Issue (ADJ) WI is not created for the RFS. ACP does not always automatically create an ADJ WI when the application is received. However, if an ROE with a contentious RFS is received during the automation process, ACP may create an ADJ WI or ROE Issue (ROE) RFS Action WI. When there is more than one ROE with the same last day paid (LDP), and one of the ROEs is contentious while the other ROE is not, adjudication is not required and both ROEs are included in the calculation. When a fraudulent payment contains an EI recoupment that has been applied to a debt that belongs to the client, the IPOC officer establishes an OP for the recoupment. The IPOC officer does not remove the recoupment amount from the tax file or T4E. In rare cases, an EI recoupment from a fraudulent payment is applied to a fraudulent OP that must be rescinded because it belongs to a third party. When a fraudulent payment contains an EI recoupment that has been applied to a third party OP that does not belong to the client because of fraudulent activities, the IPOC officer: sends the iService Recoupment Reversal Request form to National Accounts Receivable (NAR) to rescind the RW - Recoupments/Withhold document type in PSCD; rescinds the fraudulent OP in PSCD; removes the EI recoupment amount from the tax file or T4E. The IPOC officer ensures that the recoupment from the fraudulent payment is reversed in PSCD before rescinding the fraudulent OP to prevent PSCD from automatically refunding the invalid recoupment. If multiple RW document types must be reversed, the IPOC officer sends only one iService Recoupment Reversal Request form for all RW document types that must be reversed in PSCD. The IPOC officer completes the fields for one RW document type and adds all the information for the other RW document types in the Additional information field of the recoupment reversal request.

When Integrity determines that a SIN is compromised, the investigator adds a fraud warning in FTS using the FTS - Integrity Fraud Indicator transaction. When the warning is activated, the SIN field on the tombstone data is highlighted in red and a red warning symbol shows next to the field. The fraud warning remains on the file until Integrity removes it. Only Integrity investigators can add or remove the warning. The fraud warning only shows in FTS and has no impact on the other systems. It serves as an alert that the client has been a fraud victim.

When the Government of Canada introduced the EI Emergency Response Benefit (EI ERB) to provide temporary income support to workers impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic, the personal information of many Canadians was used to establish fraudulent EI ERB claims. This also occurred in the post-EI ERB period (i.e. BPC in w/c 2258 or later). The discovery of fraudulent activity in EI applications occurs in several different ways, including the following: The true SIN holder receives a T4E without having applied for benefits and contacts the call centre. A returned payment raises suspicion about a bank account. A client’s claim is transferred to another information technology centre (ITC) and the client can no longer complete claimant’s reports. A client files a new application and an officer discovers fraud indicators on a previous application while processing the claim. fraud indicators A client files a new application and a renewal is completed instead of a new claim because there is an existing fraudulent BPC. A client has an existing claim and a third party files an application and renews the client’s claim. The renewal results in the client’s banking information being changed to a bank account not owned by the client.

When a T111-10-8 is input on a claim, an invalid amount is added to the Parental field of the Tax File Adjustment (T070) transaction type 3 (T070-3) if the following conditions are met: Benefits were paid in the current tax year. There are cycling claimant’s reports on the Payments tab in FTS. For each cycling claimant’s report, the system adds $10 to the Parental field on the T070-3 that transfers the year-to-date tax amounts to the MPS tax file. The system-generated T070-3 is available the next business day on the Transaction History screen. The invalid amount is not added to the Gross Benefits field, but it is added to the Special Benefits field on the Manual Pay tab. The IPOC officer must remove the invalid parental amount from the client’s tax file with a Tax File Adjustment (T070) transaction type 2, reason C (T070-2-C) when adjusting a fraudulent claim.

Integrity refers the case to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and follows up to establish the OP on the third party’s file, if necessary. No further action is required from the processing officer related to the third party’s OP until the third party is identified. If the third party is known, the IPOC officer refers the file to a Business Expertise Advisor for guidance.

If a client is a Quebec resident, the IPOC officer determines the federal and Quebec provincial taxes when adjusting the client’s tax file. When weeks were paid to the third party in the current tax year and they must be removed or cancelled from the client’s file, the IPOC officer reviews the Payment Summary (MN19) screen in FTS for a detailed breakdown of the taxes. When requesting an amended T4E, if the third party received fraudulent payments in a previous tax year, the IPOC officer reviews the weeks paid to the third party by selecting the tax year on the Statement of benefits paid (T4E) screen. The officer then selects the Itemized Statement link for a breakdown of the taxes.

When a payment contains a third party deduction, such as an assignment of benefits (AOB), a family order agreement (FOA) or a Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) set-off, the IPOC officer does not establish an OP equal to the amount for the third party deduction because the client is not responsible for third party deduction OP resulting from fraudulent activities. If a fraudulent payment has been returned and cancelled, the IPOC officer creates an SROC to document the third party deduction amount. If the payment was issued in the current tax year, the IPOC officer also removes the third party deduction amount from the client’s file with a Tax File Adjustment ( T070) transaction. If the payment was issued in a previous tax year, the IPOC officer requests an amended T4E to remove the third party deductions from the benefits paid.

Below are the main processing steps for this activity. If the officer determines that the client knowingly made a false or misleading statement, the officer must adjudicate the availability issue, complete the record of decision (ROD), and refer to Misrepresentation to determine the type of sanction to impose. The officer must input the complete decision after determining the sanctions. Misrepresentation Reconsidering a decision EIA 52 states that a claim for benefits may be reconsidered as long as it results in an overpayment (OP) or an underpayment (UP). The time limit for reconsidering a claim is 36 months from the week benefits were paid or payable. This period is extended to 72 months if there was a false or misleading statement. EIA 52 Determining if a false statement was made A false statement is a statement that is incorrect or untrue. A false statement can be the result of an intentional or negligent action, or it can be the result of an honest mistake. For example, on the claimant’s report, a client answered Yes to the question “Were you ready, willing and capable of working each day, Monday through Friday during each week of this report?” An investigation reveals that the client was not available for work and had not been actively seeking work for the period covered by the report, because the client had no childcare. At this point, the officer only knows that the information provided by the client is incorrect. Without an explanation from the client, it cannot be determined if the client intentionally or knowingly failed to provide the correct information. Regardless of whether it was intentional or an honest mistake, clients cannot report being available for a period during which they are not due to lack of childcare; therefore, the reconsideration timeframe can be extended to 72 months. Determining if a false statement was knowingly made Knowingly means the officer can reasonably conclude that the client knew the information provided was untrue when he or she provided or did not report that information. There is no element of intent in this consideration. It is not necessary to determine a degree of fault. The officer must only establish that it is more likely that the client understood the information provided and did not accurately portray the facts. If the client received payments by paper cheque, each cheque cashed can be considered a misrepresentation under EIA 38(1)(e). If the client received payments by direct deposit, each direct deposit payment or any excess amount the client received and did not return can be considered a misrepresentation under EIA 38(1)(f). Note Reviewing a potential case of voluntary disclosure The National Policy on Voluntary Disclosure encourages clients, employers and third parties to come forward and voluntarily disclose misrepresentations. According to this policy, voluntary disclosure occurs when a person admits to having knowingly made a false statement. National Policy on Voluntary Disclosure An investigator may recommend that the file be reconsidered in light of the National Policy on Voluntary Disclosure . National Policy on Voluntary Disclosure There are 2 essential conditions for approving the voluntary disclosure: There is no investigation under way in relation to the voluntary disclosure when a client admits to making a false statement. The false statement would have resulted in punitive measures such as a penalty, a warning or prosecution had there been no voluntary disclosure. According to the National Policy on Voluntary Disclosure , there is no limit to the number of times that a client can voluntarily disclose misrepresentations. National Policy on Voluntary Disclosure

Reconsideration timeframes Under EIA 52(5), a false or misleading statement made in connection with a claim must have been made to extend the reconsideration timeframe. A false statement made regarding any contentious issue allows the extension of the reconsideration timeframe to 72 months for all contentious issues on a claim. For example, in situations in which a client did not correctly report earnings on a claimant’s report or failed to declare employment on the EI application, it is considered that the client made a false statement. Therefore, the reconsideration timeframe is extended for all issues detected, including the contentious RFS. Misrepresentation When submitting an EI application, clients are asked to declare all employment in the last 52 weeks. When declaring employment, clients are asked for the RFS. Similarly, clients who report earnings on their electronic claimant’s reports are asked if they stopped working for the employer during the reporting period. Clients who answer yes are then asked if they stopped working for a reason other than a layoff. Clients who provide incorrect information knowingly when answering questions about the RFS are making misrepresentations that warrant consideration of a sanction under EIA 38(1). Clients who do not report earnings are not asked any questions about the RFS from employment. In these cases, the officer cannot show that clients made a false statement constituting misrepresentation. The officer may find misrepresentation only when there is other evidence showing a knowingly made false statement or omission for the issue.

The investigator can request an insurability ruling in the following situations: contract of service or contract for service corporate ownership hours or earnings arm’s length 900-series SIN The CRA insurability ruling may address any of the following: the insurability of the employment the start and end date of the insurable employment the number of insurable hours of employment the amount of insurable earnings In the case of possible abuse concerning the ROE, a decision on or notice of insurability is not requested unless one of the following situations is present: It is necessary to determine the insurability of an employment or of the earnings of a specific period of employment; The employer disagrees with the changes made to the ROE as a result of the investigator’s findings; The investigator cannot find the employer or the payroll, or the information in the payroll is insufficient to determine the amount of insurable earnings or the number of insurable weekly hours. If the investigator determines that the employment situation did not exist and that the employer submitted a false ROE, an insurability ruling is not necessary. The investigator returns the file to the Level 2 officer and clearly indicates in the investigation report “false ROE — employment situation did not exist.”

Once it is determined that the client did not have just cause for voluntarily leaving the employment, the officer must determine whether an indefinite disqualification or disentitlement applies. If the client voluntarily left the employment within 3 weeks of an anticipated layoff or the end of term of employment, the 44 - Loss of employment in anticipation of layoff disentitlement (D44) is imposed. The officer imposes the D44 for a definite period only (maximum 3 weeks). If the client voluntarily left more than 3 weeks before the anticipated layoff and in all other cases, the officer imposes the 11 - Voluntary leaving - just cause not proven indefinite disqualification (D11).
