An officer can impose an indefinite 15 - Claim Procedure disentitlement (D15) when the client or the employer has not been reached and fact-finding is required to clarify the information needed to allocate the bonus. A minimum of 2 attempts at different times of day must be made to contact the client on 2 separate days. Every attempt must be documented on the file, including if a message was left. If the officer cannot reach the client by telephone or leave a message, a letter or email must be sent to request that the client contacts the officer. If the client has not been reached or cannot provide the missing information required to allocate the bonus, the officer must fact-find with the employer. If the employer cannot be contacted, is not reached or did not reply to the Z-00-00-00 letter, a D15 must be imposed. The D15 is effective from one of the following based on the claim status (CS): 0 - Active or 6 - Terminated and the claim can be reactivated: the Monday of the first cycling claimant’s report displayed on the FTS Payments tab when one of the 2 situations applies: A stop payment has been imposed for the same issue. A stop payment has been imposed for another issue and the allocation of the bonus may have an impact on cycling claimant’s reports. the Monday of the next claimant’s report to be received displayed in FTS when one of the following situations applies: No stop payment has been imposed. A stop payment has been imposed and no cycling claimant’s reports are displayed on the FTS Payments tab. A stop payment has been imposed for another issue, cycling claimant’s reports are displayed on the FTS Payments tab and the allocation of the bonus has no impact on cycling claimant’s reports. 8 - Converted to Manual Pay: Blocked or archived claim: No D15 is imposed. When a D15 is imposed, the officer sends an ACS letter to notify the client of the disentitlement and to advise the client to provide the missing information as soon as possible. Summary chart of D15 start dates: Claim in MPS When the claim is in MPS with the CS 8 - Converted to Manual Pay , the officer sends an MM06 to IPOC to impose the D15. If the claim is in MPS, it stays in MPS for the remainder of the BP and the client must complete paper claimant’s reports.

A claim can be active, terminated, blocked or archived. The claim status impacts which transactions can be input and when the letter of decision is sent: Active: The active claim is established and is currently displayed automatically in FTS. It is a claim for which benefits may be payable and that has not been terminated. Terminated: A terminated claim is showing on the Dormant tab in FTS, it has ended but can be reactivated. Once the transaction to reactivate the claim has been processed, all inputs for the allocation can be done the same way as an active claim. Blocked : In some cases, the claim that the officer must reconsider is on the Dormant tab in FTS, but the claim cannot be reactivated because there is an Active claim on the Summary screen or the BPC is older than 3 years. Adjustments to this type of claim are processed using the Blocked Claims System or, in some cases, with IPOC intervention. Archived: A claim that is no longer on the Summary screen or the Dormant tab in FTS is an archived claim. The claim, as well as previous BPC, is displayed on the Pay History (under Enquiry ). When selected, the Pay History Details will show the weeks paid and BTs paid for each BPC. Adjustments to this type of claim are also processed with IPOC intervention. Note

Allocate the monies using the following formula: If the allocation is for a monthly payment, allocate the monies as follows: Multiply the monthly amount by 12 months. Divide the result by 52 weeks. When a client comes forward to correct previously provided information or provide previously omitted information, the officer determines if the information can be considered an error correction, or if it must be referred to Integrity to be considered under the voluntary disclosure policy. To be considered an error correction, the correction must be actioned within 36 months from the week for which benefits were paid or payable. When the client is exempted from completing claimant’s reports, to be considered an error correction, the client must request the earnings correction within 6 weeks of the last payment of the exemption period was issued. The voluntary disclosure policy may apply if the client is aware that misinformation resulted in an inappropriate payment of benefits and is attempting to correct this situation. Unless specified otherwise, it is presumed that in providing the information, the client is in agreement that benefits were not payable. To determine if the new information can be considered an error correction or must be referred to Integrity, the officer refers to Determining if an issue must be referred to Integrity . Data entry varies depending on the CS. If the claim is active or is terminated but can be reactivated, the data is entered in FTS using the Allocations (M175) transaction or on the Detailed Claimant’s Report screen. If the claim is a blocked claim and the CS in BCS is 1 - Updateable , an update can be requested using BCS and the transactions can be processed. If the claim is a blocked or archived claim with a CS in BCS other than 1 - Updateable or 2 - Not blocked , the data is entered in FTS using an MM06 and is processed by IPOC. Inputs on a blocked claim — BCS BCS allows certain types of transactions to be processed on blocked dormant claims. There are 2 options available: Estimate and Claim update . Accessibility depends on the CS in BCS. BCS inputs can be done on claims with the CS 1 - Updateable . When the CS in BCS is 2 - Not blocked , the claim is reactivated to input the decision as on an active claim. For any other CS in BCS, the transactions are processed with IPOC intervention using an MM06. Claim update function When transactions must be input on a blocked claim, the Blocked Claims System tab in FTS must be reviewed to determine the CS in BCS. If the CS is 1 - Updateable , an update is requested using BCS and the transactions can be processed. Note An update in BCS can only be done on one BPC at a time. When transactions are input but not processed, Yes appears in the Block Action Pending column and access is denied for input on all other BPCs until requested transactions are processed. Access to a BPC with a pending action is limited to the officer who initiated that action. If the officer requests an update that BCS cannot complete, on the next processing day, the Blocked claim not updated or not calculated message is displayed along with the exception, error or warning on the MR05 screen. The officer reviews the exception, error or warning on the Results tab in BCS for further action. If the update cannot be completed using BCS, the system presents an estimate result. The officer sends the decision to IPOC using the Forward via MM06 link which creates the prefilled Renewal/Revised (M106) and MM06. Estimate function The Estimate function in BCS allows officers to view and evaluate the end results without processing the transactions. Estimates are possible for blocked claims with a CS 1 - Updateable as well as unblocked dormant claims, provided the CS is 05 (inactive) or 06 (terminated) . BCS Estimate transactions are processed overnight and the results are available on the Results tab the next day. Officers that have requested an estimate can view the end result and forward the request for IPOC intervention using the prefilled MM06 available under the Results tab.

When the CS in BCS is 2 - Not blocked , the officer reactivates the claim to input the decision as on an active claim. For any other CS in BCS, the transactions are processed with IPOC intervention using an MM06. Claim update function When transactions must be input on a blocked claim, the officer must review the Blocked Claims System tab in FTS to determine the CS in BCS. If the CS is 1 - Updateable , the officer requests an update using BCS and processes the transactions. Note An update in BCS can only be done on one BPC at a time. When transactions are input but not processed, Yes appears in the Block Action Pending column and access is denied for input on all other BPCs until requested transactions are processed. Access to a BPC with a pending action is limited to the officer who initiated that action. If the officer requests an update that BCS cannot complete, on the next processing day, the Blocked claim not updated or not calculated message is displayed along with the exception, error or warning on the MR05 screen. The officer reviews the exception, error or warning on the Results tab in BCS for further action. If the update cannot be completed using BCS, the system presents an estimate result. The officer sends the decision to IPOC using the Forward via MM06 link which creates the prefilled Renewal/Revised (M106) and MM06 transactions. Estimate function The Estimate function in BCS allows the officer to view and evaluate the end results without processing the transactions. Estimates are possible for blocked claims with a CS 1 - Updateable as well as unblocked dormant claims, provided the CS is 05 (inactive) or 06 (terminated) . BCS Estimate transactions are processed overnight and the results are available on the Results tab the next day. An officer who has requested an estimate can view the end result and forward the request for IPOC intervention using the prefilled MM06 available on the Results tab.

Newfoundland and Labrador — Workers’ compensation benefits (WCB) The employer is responsible for paying the first day a client is injured. The Workplace Health, Safety and Compensation Commission payments begin on the second day. There is no gap or waiting period. WCB payments are based on the client’s normal weekly work schedule. For example, if the client normally works 3 days a week, the WCB payments cover a 3-day week. Newfoundland and Labrador – Wage loss insurance (WLI) The WLI plan available to teachers in Newfoundland and Labrador is funded by the teachers and is not considered earnings for EI purposes. An officer assigned to a WI related to WLI for a Newfoundland and Labrador teacher refers to the Reassignment Guide — Instructions and reassigns the WI to a specialized unit in the Atlantic region. Reassignment Guide — Instructions Nova Scotia — Workers’ compensation benefits (WCB) The Workers’ Compensation Board of Nova Scotia pays a reduced rate for the first week of payment if the client is approved for fewer than 5 weeks at the outset. If the WCB continues beyond the 5 weeks, the client receives an adjustment. This reduction (40% of the weekly payment) is always deducted from the first payment, even if the payment is for a period greater than 5 weeks. Quebec — Paid sick leave (PSL) entitlement Residents of Quebec who have worked for an employer for 3 consecutive months are entitled to 2 full days of PSL. These amounts must be allocated even if they have not yet been paid to the client. Quebec — Workers’ compensation benefits (WCB) The Commission des normes, de l’équité, de la santé et de la sécurité du travail (CNESST) begins coverage the day following the accident. The employer pays the client for the first 14-calendar-day period or less, in accordance with the period of the incapacity, and is, in turn, reimbursed by the CNESST. The amount paid by the employer is 90% of the client’s net salary. These monies are considered a WCB amount and must be allocated as such. The employer’s coverage is for the equivalent number of days that the client would have normally worked during the 14-calendar-day pay period immediately following the accident or incapacity (work-related illness). The earnings are allocated based on the number of days the client would have worked in that period. After the 14-calendar-day period, the compensation is paid directly by the CNESST. Regardless of the client’s work schedule, the CNESST payments cover a 7-day week. Quebec — Motor vehicle accident insurance The Société d’assurance-automobile du Québec pays income replacement indemnity starting on the eighth day after the accident. The client receives the indemnity every 14 days for the period of incapacity. The indemnity represents 90% of the client’s net annual income, based on the gross annual income subject to a maximum amount. The gross annual income maximum amount is set each year. Income replacement indemnity are indexed annually on the anniversary date of the accident to keep up with the cost of living. The Société d’assurance-automobile du Québec eliminates all forms of employment contracts and bases the payment on a calculation to obtain the amount of a daily allowance payable. Therefore, regardless of the client’s work schedule, the payments cover a 7-day week. For partial or incomplete weeks, the daily allowance is multiplied by the number of days of incapacity during the week in question. When the client becomes capable of performing a job designated by the Société d’assurance-automobile du Québec and due to bodily injury, the client draws a salary lower than that from which the Société d’assurance-automobile du Québec calculated income replacement indemnity, the Société d’assurance-automobile du Québec pays the client a residual annuity to compensate for the loss of income. These monies constitute earnings because it is directly linked to the loss of income suffered by the client. For example, if the client normally works 3 days a week, the WCB payments cover a 3-day week. Saskatchewan — Workers’ compensation benefits (WCB) WCB payments are based on the client’s normal weekly work schedule. For example, if the client normally works 3 days a week, the WCB payments cover a 3-day week. Loss of income due to illness or injury may be compensated by an employer or a third party. Whether the monies are considered earnings for EI purposes depends on why the payments are made, what they are intended to compensate for and who pays them. Incapacity monies that are not considered earnings Some monies received by clients when an illness or accident occurs are not considered earnings because they are not meant to compensate for the loss of income. These include payments for pain, suffering, or disfigurement; reimbursement of prescription, medical, chiropractic, physiotherapy or daily assistance living costs; and compensation for injuries sustained while a victim of a crime. Monies received to compensate for the loss of income paid from a non-group insurance company plan are not considered as earnings. Note Incapacity monies that are considered earnings Monies paid to clients to compensate for the loss of income are considered earnings when they are paid by an employer, an insurance company or a government office. They may include paid sick leave (PSL), wage loss insurance (WLI) payments , workers' compensation benefits , motor vehicle accident benefits or payments for preventative withdrawal of services . paid sick leave wage loss insurance (WLI) payments workers' compensation benefits motor vehicle accident benefits payments for preventative withdrawal of services Note Supplementary unemployment benefits (SUB) plans Some employers have a SUB plan payable to employees who are unemployed due to illness, injury or quarantine. The purpose of these plans is to top up the difference between the amount of EI benefits paid to the employee and the employee’s regular wages. Sub plans are employment monies and are normally considered earnings. However, sub plans are reviewed at the national level to determine if they meet specific conditions to allow them to be excluded from earnings, and a list of the SUB plans meeting the conditions is kept. If a plan does not meet the conditions, the monies payable through the plan are treated as earnings and allocated to the period for which they are paid. Paid sick leave (PSL) An employer may provide a period of leave to an employee who is unable to work due to illness, injury or quarantine. Some employers may pay an employee’s salary during a period of sick leave. PSL is considered earnings. PSL prevents an interruption of earnings (I of E). However, any PSL received during the waiting period (WP) is not considered earnings. An employee’s entitlement to PSL may be based on a pre-determined amount of paid sick time allowed by the employer each year, or it may be based on a formula related to an employee’s years of service. Clients who stop working due to illness or injury and who are entitled to PSL must exhaust their sick leave credits before they are eligible to receive EI sickness benefits. If a client has an entitlement to PSL and does not apply to use it, the paid leave entitlement is still deemed earnings and is allocated to the period for which the entitlement would have been paid or payable if the client had requested the paid leave from the employer. If the employee does not have enough entitlement to cover the entire period of leave and the employer advances future sick leave entitlements to the client, the monies are still earnings and are allocated to the period for which they are paid or payable. Wage loss insurance (WLI) WLI payments are a form of compensation for the loss of wages or salary during a period of illness or injury. Whether payments from these WLI plans are considered earnings depends on whether the payments come from a group plan or a private plan purchased by a client. Group WLI plans are designed to cover a group of workers who work for the same employer. Group WLI plans are earnings. If a client who is covered by a group plan chooses not to apply for the WLI payments, the payments to which the client would have been entitled are still considered to be earnings. Payments that a client receives or is entitled to receive are allocated to the period for which the monies are paid or payable, or would have been paid or payable had the client applied to receive them. Group WLI payments do not prevent an I of E, nor are they considered to be earnings within the WP. When payments are received through a disability or sickness wage loss plan that is not a group WLI plan, the monies are specifically excluded as earnings and are not allocated. A wage loss plan that is not a group plan has the following characteristics: It cannot be related to a group of persons who are all employed by the same employer. It is not financed in whole or in part by the employer. It is voluntarily purchased by the insured person. It is completely portable, in that the rate of premium and the protection provided will remain the equivalent should the client become employed by any other employer within the same occupation. It provides constant benefits, that is, there is no provision calling for automatic benefits increments in accordance with a pre-arranged benefit schedule based on current earnings. Its premium rates are not dependent on the experience of the employer’s group of workers. Note Premium Reduction Program (PRP) Note Effective August 12, 2018, the earnings of clients receiving sickness and maternity benefits are deducted from benefits at 50% up to the earnings threshold, just as they are for clients receiving other benefit types (BTs). However, there is an exception to the changes. PSL and WLI are deducted dollar for dollar from the benefits of clients who are receiving sickness or maternity benefits and whose employer is registered in an approved PRP. For more information on how earnings deductions are calculated, the officer refers to Earnings: Earnings deduction calculation — Table . Earnings: Earnings deduction calculation — Table In order to ensure the correct amount of earnings is deducted from benefits, a premium reduction code is required when the following conditions are met: There is an allocation of PSL or WLI. The last day of PSL or of the WLI allocation is on or after August 12, 2018. If a premium reduction code is required, the officer reviews the employer’s premium reduction information in FTS. Employers enrolled in the PRP have been granted a reduction of their payable EI premiums because they have demonstrated that they provide their employees with a specific amount of PSL or WLI benefits that meets the standards of the PRP. The details of the PRP are available in the Employer Details screen in FTS and are used to determine if the employer paying WLI or PSL has an approved plan. Many employers have multiple business numbers. Whenever possible, it is important to search for the employer using the business number indicated on the ROE, as not all business numbers have the same entitlement to employee benefits. To determine if the employer is enrolled in the PRP, the officer checks the Status field on the Premium Reduction Program tab on the Employer Details screen in FTS. A Reduction status indicates that the employer is enrolled in the PRP. The most recent input for a calendar year is the current premium reduction plan status of the employer. Any time there is a change to the employer’s plan, a new line is added with the relevant status. Status 1 means the employer has an approved plan. Status 3, 4, 7 and 9 mean that the employer still has an approved plan but there may be some changes pending in the PRP system. Status 5 means that the employer currently has a plan but that it will end on December 31 of the year in question. Note Workers’ compensation benefits (WCB) Workers who develop a work-related illness or who are injured on the job may be entitled to compensation for that illness or injury by a provincial workers’ compensation board. These payments are funded by contributions made by the employer and may provide not only compensation for loss of income but also for other expenses and allowances. Lump sums and pensions that are paid in full and final settlement of workers’ compensation claims are not considered earnings and are not allocated. While only full and final settlements of a claim are specifically excluded as earnings, payments that are not intended to replace the client’s lost income are also not considered earnings. These payments may include reimbursement of medical, chiropractic or physiotherapy costs; costs for obtaining attendant care to assist with daily living; and prescription costs. Monies paid in compensation for permanent impairment, disfigurement or the loss of enjoyment of life directly related to the illness or injury are not considered earnings because they are paid in full and final settlement and are not related to the client’s loss of income. Monies paid by workers’ compensation boards are considered earnings if their purpose is to compensate a client for loss of income due to the incapacity and are not made in a full and final settlement. Temporary income support is paid during the initial stages of an illness or injury and usually continues until either the client recovers, or it is determined that the client is unlikely to recover. It is only at that time that a full and final settlement may be made. Workers’ compensation payments intended as income support are allocated to the period for which they are paid or payable. The payments do not prevent an I of E, nor are they considered as earnings within the WP. Motor vehicle accident benefits Individuals who are involved in automobile accidents may receive payments through insurance provided under provincial law or by a commercial insurance company. Payments for pain, suffering, disfigurement, or medical expenses are not intended as income replacement and are therefore not considered earnings. Payments made in compensation for an actual or presumed loss of income may be considered earnings, depending on who makes the payments and whether EI benefits are taken into account in their calculation. Payments made to a person from a commercial insurance company that are not provided under a provincial law are not considered earnings. Payments from governmental motor vehicle insurance plans are considered earnings if EI benefits are not taken into account when determining the amount that is payable to the client. If benefits are taken into account, the monies paid are not considered earnings. Payments from provincial motor vehicle insurance plans that do not take EI into account when determining the amount payable are allocated to the weeks for which these amounts are payable regardless of when they are paid. If the client is entitled to compensation but does not apply for it, the payments are still considered earnings. The amount of the compensation that could have been paid, as well as the period it would have covered, are determined according to what would appear most probable under the circumstances. Motor vehicle accident compensation payments are not considered earnings when they are meant to cover a period after the accident in which the client has accumulated enough hours of insurable employment to establish a benefit period (BP). However, it is not necessary that a new BP be established. Motor vehicle accident insurance payments are not considered earnings when they meet one of the following criteria: They are purchased by the client from a private insurance company in the following provinces: Alberta New Brunswick Newfoundland and Labrador Northwest Territories Nova Scotia Nunavut Prince Edward Island Yukon They are paid according to provincial law to compensate for pain, suffering, disfigurement or medical expenses. They are paid according to provincial law to compensate for vehicle or property damage. They are paid according to provincial law to compensate for loss of income, and EI benefits are deducted before the payment is issued to the client. Preventative withdrawal payments Preventative measures may be taken when working conditions present physical danger to an employee’s health, danger to an unborn child or to a child the employee is breast-feeding. While the employee may not be incapacitated, she could become incapacitated or unemployed if these measures were not taken. In such cases, if the employer is unable to assign the employee to another job, compensation may be payable to her under provincial labour legislation for the period of the withdrawal of the employee’s services. Any payment received for withdrawal of services as a preventative measure is considered earnings if benefits under the EIA are not taken into account when calculating the amount to be paid under the provincial legislation. Even if clients choose not to apply for the payments to which they are entitled under the provincial law, any entitlement under that provincial law is still considered earnings. Payments that are made for the withdrawal of services as a preventative measure are allocated to the weeks for which those payments are paid or payable, or for which they would have been paid or payable for if the client had applied. Accumulated sick leave paid on termination of employment The payment of accumulated sick leave credits is a form of compensation for all or a portion of an employee’s unused sick leave. When paid on termination of employment, these monies are not paid to compensate for incapacity but are paid because of a layoff or separation. If accumulated sick leave is paid to clients on termination of employment, the officer refers to Allocating monies on separation . Allocating monies on separation

An officer can impose an indefinite 15 - Claim Procedure disentitlement (D15) when the client or the employer has not been reached and fact-finding is required to clarify the information needed to allocate incapacity monies. A minimum of 2 attempts at different times of day must be made to contact the client on 2 separate days. Every attempt must be documented on the file, including if a message was left. If the officer cannot reach the client by telephone or leave a message, a letter or email must be sent to request that the client contacts the officer. If the client has not been reached or cannot provide the missing information required to allocate incapacity monies and incapacity monies are paid by an employer, the officer must fact-find with the employer. If the employer cannot be contacted, is not reached or did not reply to the Z-00-00-00 letter, a D15 must be imposed. When the claim status (CS) in FTS is 0 - Active , 6 - Terminated (and the claim can be reactivated) or 8 - Converted to Manual Pay , the D15 is effective from the Monday of the renewal week. When the claim is blocked or archived, no D15 is imposed. The goal of all pension plans is to pay pension benefits on a periodic basis (annuity) on retirement. However, there are 3 reasons why a client may receive a lump-sum payment instead of an annuity: The payments are below a certain minimum level. The life expectancy of a client is shortened. There is a special “unlocking” of previously locked-in pension credits. This is allowed by some pension plans when a client leaves the employment before retirement age. This is not the same as a return of employee contributions, which happens before the pension credits are locked in. Any other lump-sum payment that resulted from a retirement or separation, outside the terms of the pension plan, and without immediate pension entitlement according to the terms of the pension plan, is probably a lump-sum payment made on separation. Because these retirement payments result from a layoff or separation, they are allocated from the week of the layoff or separation at normal weekly earnings. If a lump-sum payment is made on separation, the officer refers to Allocating monies on separation , Allocating monies on separation — Renewal claim or Modifying the allocation of monies on separation . Allocating monies on separation Allocating monies on separation — Renewal claim Modifying the allocation of monies on separation Allocating lump-sum pensions When a pension has been paid in a lump-sum, it is meant to compensate clients in the same way a pension paid as an annuity would for the balance of the client’s life. Once a lump-sum pension is payable, the monies are considered earnings for EI purposes and must be allocated, regardless of what the client chooses to do with them. Lump-sum pension payments must be converted to the equivalent of what they would have been if they had been paid as an annuity. This is vastly different than the allocation of other lump-sums paid on separation at normal weekly earnings. To ensure that the lump-sum pension payment is converted correctly, the calculation is performed using the appropriate tables to convert lump-sum pension benefit into a life annuity. If the lump-sum pension was paid or became payable before June 7, 2015, the officer refers to Schedule II to find the appropriate weekly annuity equivalent for the client’s age. Schedule II If the lump-sum pension was paid on June 7, 2015, or became payable after, the officer refers to Digest 5.13.6.4 — Allocation of a lump-sum pension benefit to find the appropriate weekly annuity equivalent for the client’s age. The Table: Weekly annuity equivalents for a lump sum of $1,000 according to age of claimant displays the current and 2 previous years. The officer refers to Amendments to the Digest of Benefit Entitlement Principles for the previous years. Digest 5.13.6.4 — Allocation of a lump-sum pension benefit Table: Weekly annuity equivalents for a lump sum of $1,000 according to age of claimant Amendments to the Digest of Benefit Entitlement Principles The annuity equivalent amount for each $1 000 of the lump-sum payment is determined by the client’s age at the time that the lump-sum was paid. The lump-sum amount is then divided by 1 000, and the resulting figure is multiplied by the annuity equivalent amount. Example

An officer can impose an indefinite 15 - Claim Procedure disentitlement (D15) when the client has not been reached and fact-finding is required to clarify the information needed to allocate the lump-sum or periodic pension. If the client has not been reached or cannot provide the missing information required to allocate the lump-sum or periodic pension, a D15 must be imposed. The D15 is effective from one of the following based on the CS: 0 - Active or 6 - Terminated and the claim can be reactivated: the Monday of the first cycling claimant’s report displayed in the FTS Payments tab when one of the 2 situations applies: A stop payment has been imposed for the same issue. A stop payment has been imposed for another issue and the allocation of the lump-sum or periodic pension has an impact on cycling claimant’s reports. the Monday of the next claimant’s report to be received displayed in FTS when one of the following situations applies: No stop payment has been imposed. A stop payment has been imposed and no cycling claimant’s reports are displayed on the FTS Payments tab. A stop payment has been imposed for another issue, cycling claimant’s reports are displayed on the FTS Payments tab and the allocation of the lump-sum or periodic pension has no impact on cycling claimant’s reports. 8 - Converted to Manual Pay: The Monday following the week displayed in the Last claimant’s report processed field of the Manual Pay tab in FTS. Blocked or archived claim: No D15 is imposed. When a D15 is imposed, the officer sends an ACS letter to notify the client of the disentitlement and to advise the client to provide the missing information as soon as possible. Summary chart of D15 start dates: Claim in MPS When the claim is in MPS with the CS 8 - Converted to Manual Pay , the officer sends an MM06 to IPOC to impose the D15. If the claim is in MPS, it stays in MPS for the remainder of the BP and the client must complete paper claimant’s reports.

Pensions that are paid based on contributions to a plan by the employer, the client or both are earnings for benefits purposes. Pension payments are linked to the client’s employment because the employment made the pension payments possible. This is true whether the monies are paid in a lump-sum or whether they are paid on a periodic basis (annuity), and regardless of what the client chooses to do with the monies. Pension payments from the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) or other provisional plans are also paid based on contributions made by the client while working for an employer and are also considered earnings for benefit purposes. Note Pensions that are not considered earnings An employer may choose to provide a disability pension to employees who are not able to work. Disability pensions of any type, whether they are received from an employer or through the CPP or the Quebec Pension Plan, are not considered earnings. However, the disability plan must be examined to determine if it is actually a disability pension or whether it is a disability wage loss insurance plan, as the latter is considered earnings and must be allocated accordingly. Other examples of pensions that are not related to employment and are not considered earnings are: survivor’s or dependant’s pension Old Age Security pension and supplement allowances paid to veterans under the War Veterans Allowance Act pensions from divorce settlements additional voluntary contributions privately purchased pension plans Retirement pensions A pension plan is a formal agreement between employer and employees to provide a pension benefit on retirement. Pension plans may also pay other monies on termination of employment before retirement. To determine whether these monies are earnings, and to properly allocate any earnings, the officer must understand the basic provisions of pension plans and the relevant legislation under which these plans are registered and operate. There is an explanation of some of the common terms used in pension plans and legislation in the section Pension Plan Terminology of the Digest. Pension Plan Terminology A pension benefit, whether in an annuity or lump-sum form, cannot be received until the client establishes that he or she has locked-in pension credits, reaches a retirement age as specified in the plan, and applies for the pension. Pension paid or payable Allocation of pension monies considered to be earnings cannot start until these monies are paid or are payable. Therefore the officer must determine when pension monies are paid or become payable. This information can be obtained by reviewing the details of the pension plan, pension legislation and information provided by the employer about the client’s entitlement. Pension monies that have been received by the client are considered as paid. For EI purposes, payable means that legal entitlement to these monies exists and that these monies are immediately due. The due date is found in the terms and conditions of the pension plan. The conditions state the normal retirement age, early retirement age, and any monies due on termination if a pension is not immediately payable. Some plans make provisions for the payment of the pension to be deferred until the client applies for it, even if the client has reached normal retirement age. If the client has that choice under the plan and exercises it, the monies cannot be considered payable until the client applies for the pension, and the allocation of these monies starts at that time.

Once clients have reached normal retirement age or an early retirement age as specified in the pension plan, clients may apply to start their pension payments. At that time, the locked-in pension credits are used to pay the pension. When a pension is paid as an annuity, a fixed sum is paid on a periodic basis, usually monthly. For EI purposes, pension credits paid as an annuity are referred to as a periodic pension. Many employers’ pension plans, the CPP and the Quebec Pension Plan are paid as an annuity. Pension bridging benefits Employers may offer pension bridging benefits to employees who have been forced to retire early and are not yet eligible to receive their pension or who have received a reduced pension amount due to the early retirement. Pension bridging benefits may also be offered as an incentive to early retirement. Pension bridging benefits provide clients with monies that would not be payable until a later date and helps with the transition to the retirement date. Pension bridging benefits are paid until the pension entitlement is reached. These benefits may be used as a top-up to a pension payment where the pension amount is reduced due to forced early retirement. The benefit is structured so that the total amount of monies received each month remains constant. Because a pension bridging benefit is considered earnings from employment, is paid at retirement age, and is usually calculated based on the employee’s age, years of service and retirement date, it is treated and allocated as a retirement pension for EI purposes. A pension bridging benefit has the following characteristics: It bridges to future pension entitlement (company pension, CPP, Quebec Pension Plan, Old Age Security). The amount of the bridging benefit is based on a periodic payment. The individual receiving the benefit has reached retirement age (either early or normal). The amount paid is similar to the future pension payment. If the pension bridging benefits are paid out of general company revenues, there are 3 additional conditions that must be met: The bridging benefit payment period does not count towards years of service for the company pension that is to be paid. The employer’s bridging benefit program must be based on the worker meeting a set age, years of service and retirement date requirements. The bridging benefit payment must not reduce the individual’s entitlement to severance payments accumulated from that employment according to the contract or collective agreement or provincial or federal labor standards. Allocating periodic pensions or pension bridging benefits The gross amount of the periodic pension must be allocated. This includes the basic pension amount and any supplement to that pension, including pension bridging benefits. It also includes any deductions made for the purpose of buying back previous service or non-existent service under the terms of the pension plan. If the exact amount of the gross pension is not known at the time of allocation, an estimate is used. The client is advised to provide the correct amount as soon as possible. Periodic pensions are usually paid monthly but are allocated on a weekly basis. Monthly periodic pensions are converted to a weekly amount by multiplying the monthly amount by 12 to obtain the yearly figure and then dividing the result by 52 to obtain the weekly amount for allocation. If pension payments start on a day other than the beginning of a week (Monday), the weekly amount is prorated for the number of working days the pension was payable (one fifth for each working day).

The Post-Retirement Benefit is an additional benefit available to people who are already receiving CPP benefits. Clients who work while receiving CPP benefits can continue to make contributions to the CPP based on work done after the start of CPP benefits. These clients are then eligible for an additional amount from CPP — the Post-Retirement Benefit. Post-Retirement Benefit In January of each year, a client’s eligibility for an additional Post-Retirement Benefit amount is determined based on the employment from the previous year, and the new combined CPP and Post-Retirement Benefit amount is calculated. The Post-Retirement Benefit is considered earnings according to EIR 35(2)(e) and must be allocated. This applies even if the current CPP allocation (including any current Post-Retirement Benefit) is a re-qualified pension. EIR 35(2)(e) The Post-Retirement Benefit can also become a re-qualified pension if the 3 conditions noted above are met. Note

Quebec Pension Plan The Quebec Pension Plan is a compulsory public pension plan for Quebec residents, it replaces the CPP. Retirement, Post-Retirement, disability and death benefits are offered by the Quebec Pension Plan, but for EI purposes only the retirement and Post-Retirement benefits are considered earnings. Quebec Pension Plan retirement benefits must be allocated in the same way that all other periodic pension benefits are. It is very rare for a client to receive both Quebec Pension Plan and CPP benefits on one claim. In that case, the monies are never allocated to the same period, but one after the other according to when they were received. Refunds of contributions — Quebec In Quebec, clients can receive a refund of the monies that were paid into a pension fund. If a client states that a refund from a pension plan was received, the refund is allocated as a lump-sum pension benefit if one of the following two scenarios applies: If the client gets a refund that is less than 20% of the maximum pensionable earnings, determine the maximum pensionable earnings amount . maximum pensionable earnings amount If the client reaches the age of 65 and receives a refund that is less than or equal to 40% of the maximum pensionable earnings, determine the maximum pensionable earnings amount . maximum pensionable earnings amount For more information on this subject, the officer refers to Quebec Pension Plan (QPP) . While the intent of all pension plans is to pay a pension benefit when an employee retires, sometimes the employment ends before the employee reaches retirement age. If the employee has worked a certain amount of time according to the provisions of the plan, the contributions are non-refundable and locked in until retirement age. If the employee leaves the employment for any reason before the contributions are locked in, the contributions and interest are paid to the employee on termination of the employment. When termination of employment before the normal age of retirement or early retirement occurs, clients may receive a return of their contributions on separation from the employment. As pensions can be funded by either the employer or employee or both, how the return of contributions is treated for benefit purposes depends on whether the employee or the employer made the contributions. Return of employee contributions In all cases where employee contributions are returned to the employee on termination, they are still considered to be earnings from employment for EI purposes. However, since they are part of the employee’s gross weekly earnings during employment, they are considered as earnings during the period of employment. As a result, the return of employee contributions on termination of employment has no effect on any current period. Return of employer contributions Employer contributions to the pension fund are made for the periods of employment. Employer contributions can be made into a pension fund by matching employee contributions or as a fixed amount per employee, a percentage of the employee’s earnings, or a percentage of the employer’s profits for a period. Employer contributions are not part of the employee’s gross wages and are not used in the calculation of the employee’s income tax, CPP or EI premiums. Once a separation from employment occurs, if the employer’s contributions are not locked in, the contributions are paid to the employee. Because these earnings were paid due to a layoff or separation, they must be allocated as a termination payment at normal weekly earnings starting with the week of layoff or separation. The officer refers to Allocating monies on separation to allocate these earnings. Allocating monies on separation

A permanent separation can occur later than the LDW during the BP (e.g. severance pay is paid due to a permanent closure that occurred during the temporary layoff). When clients receive separation monies because of a later separation, the earnings allocation starts on the week of the actual separation rather than on the LDW. When the allocation starts the week of the permanent separation, the officer determines the amount to allocate using the following formula: Divide the separation monies by the NWE. The result is the number of weeks for the allocation. Take the number of full weeks of allocation and multiply that number by the NWE. Subtract that total from the total amount of separation monies paid. The balance, if any, is allocated to the next week.

When the client receives separation monies because of a temporary layoff or a permanent separation from employment and the LDW coincides with the layoff or separation date, the allocation starts from that date. For an initial claim or when processing a recalculation because an amended ROE was received, UIC automatically allocates the separation monies from the BPC according to the information on the ROE. For continuing and renewal claims, the officer determines if the earnings last week worked (ELWW) are less than the NWE, according to the client’s information. If yes and the allocation starts in the last week worked, the officer determines the amount to allocate using the following formula: Subtract the ELWW from the NWE. The difference is the amount that must be topped up with separation monies. This amount is allocated in the last week worked. Subtract the amount of separation monies that was used to top up the final week from the total separation monies paid. Divide the balance of the separation monies by the NWE. The result is the number of full weeks of allocation at the NWE. Take the number of full weeks of allocation and multiply that number by the NWE. Subtract that total from the amount determined in step 2 of this formula. The balance, if any, is allocated to the next week. If the ELWW are equal to or greater than the NWE and the allocation starts the week following the LDW, the officer determines the amount to allocate using the following formula: Divide the separation monies by the NWE. The result is the number of full weeks of allocation at the NWE. Take the number of full weeks of allocation and multiply that number by the NWE. Subtract that total from the total amount of separation monies paid. The balance, if any, is allocated to the next week.

The officer refers to Determining if monies are earnings . Determining if monies are earnings Note Budget 2021 A Budget 2021 measure applies to separation monies that are reviewed between September 26, 2021 (w/c 2310) and September 24, 2022 (w/c 2361) and are paid due to a temporary layoff or a permanent separation from employment. When separation monies are reviewed during that period, they are not considered earnings and are not allocated, regardless of the BPC. Separation monies that are not allocated cannot extend a benefit period (BP). This measure applies to all benefit types (BTs) for initial, renewal and continuing claims and to the following types of monies if they are paid due to layoff or separation: vacation pay pay in lieu of notice severance pay retirement allowance and retirement leave credits sick leave credits closure bonus separation or retirement bonus settlement payments If it is clear that the monies are separation monies, no fact-finding is required. However, it is still necessary to conduct fact-finding and enter the information properly on the ROE for monies such as bonuses, sick leave credits, settlement pay, and preventive withdrawal payments. If the monies are paid because of the separation, the officer leaves the date fields of the ROE blank and Unemployment Insurance Calculation (UIC) does not allocate the monies. If the monies are paid for any other reason, the officer enters the appropriate dates in the ROE, and UIC allocates the amounts as usual. Vacation pay that is paid on separation is not allocated. All other vacation pay (e.g. vacation pay that is included with each pay or that is paid on a specific date each year) is allocated according to regular procedures. As of September 25, 2022 (w/c 2362), separation monies are again considered earnings and a transitional provision applies to ensure that clients are not penalized by a late review. New allocations with an allocation start date on or after September 25, 2022 (w/c 2362) apply to initial, renewal and continuing claims and could extend the BP, if necessary. Modifying an existing allocation When modifying an existing allocation, the rules that applied to that claim when the allocation was initially input still apply. Transitional provision As of September 25, 2022 (w/c 2362), when reviewing separation monies, if the allocation start date is between September 26, 2021 (w/c 2310) and September 24, 2022 (w/c 2361), monies paid or payable due to a temporary layoff or a permanent separation from employment are not considered earnings and are not allocated. The allocation start date is the date the allocation would start, even if no BP was established for that period. BE Memo 2022-04 – Roll back of temporary measures of Budget 2021 - Seeing Canadians and Businesses through to Recovery Separation monies that are not considered earnings The reimbursement of job related expenses, costs, the payment of job-related allowances and returns on investments are not considered earnings when they do not represent a gain or benefit. This includes relocation costs as well as tuition and book costs for retraining. In cases where the employer has provided a payment for job searching or job training costs which have not yet been incurred, if the client demonstrates a genuine intent to use the monies for their intended purpose, they are not considered earnings. The return of the employee’s own pension plan contributions if the pension is not locked in, while considered earnings, has no impact at the time of separation as they were part of the employee’s gross earnings while employed and would have been considered earnings at that time. Separation monies that are considered earnings Monies that can be paid or payable on separation include monies that are payable as a form of compensation for the loss of employment, such as wages in lieu of notice, severance pay and retirement payments. Other monies can also be owing to an employee at the time of separation. Some examples of these are vacation pay, unused sick leave credits, bonuses and statutory holiday pay. Note Note Note Pay in lieu of notice By law, an employer must always provide notice of a layoff to the affected employees in a timely manner. When notice cannot be given in time, an employer can pay wages in lieu of notice. Provincial legislation usually specifies the minimum amount of notice that must be given to employees. However, company policy, collective agreements and in some cases, the circumstances of the layoff can provide for a greater notice period. Employers can choose to give notice to the affected employees and have them work throughout the notice period, or release the employees immediately and pay wages in lieu of notice, or have the employees work during the notice period and pay wages in lieu of notice. In some cases, an employer can choose to pay wages in lieu of notice even if there is no requirement to do so, such as in the case of a dismissal with cause. In some provinces, when a layoff is expected to be temporary, even if it is for more than the minimum notice required by the provincial legislation, the payment of notice can be deferred. When the layoff has exceeded the minimum notice period, the layoff is no longer considered temporary and wages in lieu of notice, if not yet paid, become payable. In this case, it is necessary to determine what event triggered the payment; the initial layoff or the permanent separation from employment. The wages in lieu of notice are allocated from the date of the event that triggered the payment. Decisions regarding the allocation of wages in lieu of notice must be made on a case-by-case basis, in accordance with the applicable employment standards, and the specific facts. Whether wages in lieu of notice become payable upon the temporary layoff or upon a permanent separation from employment depends on the applicable employment standards legislation. If the initial layoff is permanent, regardless of when wages in lieu of notice are actually paid, the monies are allocated from the date of the initial layoff. If the provincial or territorial employment standards consider that wages in lieu of notice are only payable upon a permanent separation from employment, the earnings are allocated from the date of permanent separation. In some provincial legislation, the date of termination is considered to be the date of the initial temporary layoff, if the layoff period exceeds the maximum legal period of a temporary layoff. In those cases, the earnings are allocated from the week of the initial layoff. If the employer pays wages in lieu of notice during a period when the layoff remains temporary (i.e. no termination has occurred), the payment is allocated from the date of the initial layoff. Severance pay Severance pay is paid to compensate for the loss of employment and is generally only paid when there is a complete termination of the employer-employee relationship. It is a form of recognition for years of service. Collective agreements or company policy may contain a clause requiring the payment of severance pay in certain circumstances. Severance pay can also be paid to comply with provincial legislative requirements and in this case, is based on a formula related to years of service. When it is known that the separation is permanent at the time of the layoff, severance monies can be paid at that time, and in that case, the monies are allocated from the LDW. However in many cases, severance pay can be paid to employees when they have not been recalled to work after a designated number of weeks or months has passed. Provincial legislation states that a separation occurs at that time, and requires the payment of severance pay. In this scenario, both a layoff and a separation have occurred at different times. Severance pay is payable because of the separation, which occurred only after a certain period of time passed, and not because of the layoff. In this case the severance pay would be allocated from the week of the separation from employment. Retirement payments Some employers may choose to provide a retirement payment to employees on separation. This is different than the payment of a retirement pension. This type of payment does not mean that the employee has retired or is even of retirement age. It is a payment that can be made as a form of severance payment, a payment in lieu of severance pay or even as a payment to increase the severance package. It can be paid as a lump sum on separation or in the form of periodic payments. The payment can be based on years of service or on a formula related to the amount of time an employee has left before retirement. The payment can be a gratuity based on the circumstances of the separation or an early retirement incentive. This type of benefit can take many different forms. The employer can give the employee a leave of absence with full or reduced pay. In the case of a salary continuance, a client’s status as an employee continues and the payment of the salary prevents an interruption of earnings from that employment. The monies are allocated to the period for which they are payable. Another type of retirement payment is a periodic payment given to an employee as a retirement incentive after the separation has occurred and can equal the amount the employee’s pension payment would be. While this is a type of bridging benefit, it does not meet the definition of a pension bridging benefit. A return of all or a portion of the employer’s pension plan contributions that are not locked in are also considered to be a retirement benefit. As the event that resulted in the payment of these monies is the layoff or separation, the monies are deemed earnings on separation. Vacation pay When an employee is laid off or terminated, any unpaid vacation leave is paid out. With the exception of vacation pay put into a trust fund, it does not matter when the vacation pay was earned or paid; the allocation starts from the week the layoff or separation occurred. Clients can request the payment of their vacation pay before a layoff or a separation so that their entitlement to EI benefits is not affected. However, since it is the layoff or separation that prompted the payment of the vacation pay, the allocation still starts from the week the layoff or separation occurred. Accumulated sick leave paid on termination of employment The payment of accumulated sick leave credits is a form of compensation for all or a portion of an employee’s unused sick leave. When paid on termination of employment, these monies are not paid to compensate for incapacity but are paid because of a layoff or separation. The earnings are allocated from the week of the separation from employment. Wage Earner Protection Program (WEPP) When an employer is unable to pay wages or separation monies due to bankruptcy, a client can apply to receive monies to compensate for the loss of income through WEPP. If the client reports receiving monies from WEPP, the officer must refer to Allocating Wage Earner Protection Program monies . Allocating Wage Earner Protection Program monies

NWE are the earnings gained on a regular basis at that employment. Earnings are allocated based on the NWE on continuing and renewal claims. UIC calculates the average NWE for initial claims. The NWE is usually provided by the client on the EI application (renewal application), or is indicated on an SROC or an Action Item (AI) WI on a continuing claim. If this information is not indicated in the file, the officer obtains it from the client or employer. This statement must be accepted as given. NWE are calculated depending on how the client is paid: Employees paid by the hour: Multiply the number of hours normally worked per week by the hourly rate of pay. Employees paid monthly: Multiply the gross amount earned per month by 12 and divide it by 52 to determine the weekly amount. Employees paid annually: Divide the gross annual salary by 52 weeks to determine the weekly amount. Contract employees: Divide the gross amount earned in the contract by the number of weeks included in the contract period.

When clients receive separation monies, the nature of the monies paid or payable must be examined to determine if the monies are considered to be earnings from employment. Separation monies are intended to compensate for the loss of wages and benefits related to that employment. Unless the client is able to show that the monies received on separation are not intended to compensate for the loss of wages or benefits related to the employment, the monies are considered to be earnings from employment and paid or payable on separation. Once that determination has been made, the monies are considered earnings and must be allocated. Normally, the LDW coincides with the layoff or separation and the allocation starts from that date. However, in some cases, a separation can occur during a period of a layoff that had been temporary. In those cases, the officer must determine whether the monies were paid for the layoff or the separation. If the monies are paid or payable because of the later separation, the allocation of the earnings starts on the date of the actual separation rather than the layoff. An employer can defer the payment of monies that are payable because of financial difficulties or a client may want to defer payment for tax purposes. The date the payment is received is not taken into account when allocating separation monies. Employees can choose to use their separation monies to purchase Registered Retirement Savings Plans (RRSPs), to have the employer deposit the monies directly into an RRSP, or to have the monies deposited directly into their pension plan to purchase additional credits or increase their pension. Regardless of what the client chooses to do with the monies, they are monies paid due to separation and must be allocated from the date of the separation.

When an employer-employee relationship ends, whether temporarily or permanently, employees have rights and entitlements through employment laws and in some cases, employer policy or union contracts. Employees have the right to notice of an impending layoff, and when notice is not given, payment in lieu of notice. When the separation is permanent, employees can also be entitled to other forms of compensation. Layoff A separation from an employer can be due to a permanent separation or a temporary layoff. A layoff normally refers to a temporary cessation of work, a shortage of work or a general vacation period. During a layoff period, the employee often retains recall or seniority rights. The layoff can last for only a few days or it can be a substantial period of time. Permanent separation A permanent separation refers to the final and complete severance of the employer-employee relationship. Usually it is caused by a dismissal, a restructuring, a closure or a voluntary separation. A separation can occur immediately on the last day worked (LDW). It can also occur during a layoff when recall rights expire or are surrendered or, it can be the result of an event unrelated to the original cessation of work, such as a later decision to close the place of business. In either case, clients may receive monies to compensate for the loss of employment, such as wages in lieu of notice or severance pay or monies that are owed to them, such as accumulated sick leave credits or vacation pay. Clients may also receive returns on investments or monies to reimburse job related expenses.

Remuneration under a contract of employment for the performance of services is part of the entire income arising out of any employment. It includes those moneys that are paid for the services that an employee provides to an employer. Remuneration for the performance of services includes such payments as wages or salary, fringe benefits, shift bonuses and shift premiums, overtime, stand-by hours, commissions, isolation pay or northern allowances, or call-back pay. However, retroactive increases in wages or salary are specifically excluded from consideration as earnings. Allocation under EIR 36(4) Other monies allocated under EIR 36(4) are directly related to the performance of services. Therefore, they are allocated to the period in which the services were performed. For example, overtime worked that is immediately paid to the employee is directly related to the performance of services. Accumulated overtime that could not be taken as leave due to a layoff is allocated to the period in which the services were performed. However, if the accumulated overtime was taken as leave, it is allocated to the period of the leave as this is now the reason for the payment of the money. EIR 36(4)

Remuneration payable under a contract of employment without requiring that an employee directly perform services in exchange for that particular payment meets the character of a compensation for work if the entitlement to the payment arises because of the terms and conditions of the employment contract. In addition, earnings which are payable in consideration of a client's returning to or commencing work with an employer are allocated to the period for which they are payable (i.e. the client fulfills all the required conditions and returns to or commences work). If the employee must return to work for a specific period of time before being entitled to the payment for returning to work, then the period for which it is payable is the week of the return to work. Allocation under EIR 36(5) Other monies allocated under EIR 36(5) are not directly related to the performance of services and are allocated to the period for which they are payable. For example, overtime that is taken as compensatory leave is accumulated at the time the services were performed. However, the overtime is banked until the employee takes leave. In this situation, the overtime is now directly related to the event, which is the taking of the leave. EIR 36(5)

This task deals with allocating SE earnings once a decision has been rendered and the client is considered minor in extent. If a decision has not been rendered regarding the client’s SE status, the officer refers to Self-employment . Self-employment Self-employment (SE) is minor in extent A self-employed person can acquire hours of insurable employment from other employment and qualify for benefits or a client can start SE activities while on claim. Generally, a self-employed person is regarded as a person who works a full work week (FWW), and therefore is not unemployed. However, when the SE activity is so minor in extent that a person would not normally rely upon it as a principal means of livelihood, the client is regarded as not working a FWW and any earnings from the SE activities are considered. The officer must only consider the earnings when the decision on the SE issue has been adjudicated and considered minor in extent.

SE involves income generating activities such as providing a product, offering a service on one’s behalf or managing persons who attempt to generate that income. As long as the client is engaged in the operation of the business, the monies resulting from that SE are earnings. SE means working on one’s own behalf rather than being employed by someone else. SE can take different forms: independent work or contracting working under a contract for service farming or owning part of a farming business sole proprietorship partnership (general or limited) co-adventure corporation or limited company A self-employed worker works under a contract for services rather than under a contract of service (as an employee). Examples of self-employed workers include: tradespersons truck owners taxi drivers real estate salespeople salespeople elected public officials professionals (e.g. doctor, accountant, lawyer) Farming consists of being engaged in occupational activities of operating a farm and is subject to the same regulatory provisions as operating any other business, whether self-employed as a sole proprietor, a partner or a co-adventurer.

When the client receives vacation pay because of a temporary layoff or a permanent separation from employment and the LDW coincides with the layoff or separation date, the allocation starts from that date. For an initial claim or when processing a recalculation because an amended ROE was received, UIC automatically allocates the vacation pay from the BPC according to the information on the ROE. For continuing and renewal claims, the officer determines if the ELWW are less than the NWE, according to the client’s information. If yes and the allocation starts in the last week worked, the officer determines the amount to allocate using the following formula: Subtract the ELWW from the NWE. The difference is the amount that must be topped up with the vacation pay. This amount is allocated in the last week worked. Subtract the amount of vacation pay that was used to top up the final week from the total vacation pay paid. Divide the balance of the vacation pay by the NWE. The result is the number of full weeks of allocation at the NWE. Take the number of full weeks of allocation and multiply that number by the NWE. Subtract that total from the amount determined in step 2 of this formula. The balance, if any, is allocated to the next week. If the ELWW are equal to or greater than the NWE and the allocation starts the week following the LDW, the officer determines the amount to allocate using the following formula: Divide the vacation pay by the NWE. The result is the number of full weeks of allocation at the NWE. Take the number of full weeks of allocation and multiply that number by the NWE. Subtract that total from the total amount of vacation pay paid. The balance, if any, is allocated to the next week.

Vacation pay is income from employment and is considered earnings. The only exception is vacation pay accumulated in an approved trust fund. When clients report receiving vacation pay, the officer reviews the reason for the payment of the vacation pay to determine how the vacation pay must be allocated. The law requires employers to pay vacation pay to employees. Under provincial legislation, there is a minimum amount that employers must pay as a percentage of the employee’s gross wage or salary. The purpose of vacation pay is to allow employees to receive payment during periods of vacation or rest. However, not all employees who receive vacation pay are entitled to time off work for vacation leave and vacation pay may be paid under circumstances other than a specific vacation period. Note Note Vacation pay that is paid because of a separation or layoff When an employee is laid off or terminated, any unpaid vacation leave is paid out. Allocation starts from the week the layoff or separation occurred. When clients request the payment of their vacation pay in anticipation of a layoff or a separation, the allocation still starts on the week of the layoff or separation. Once it is determined that the vacation pay is payable because of a layoff or separation from employment, the monies are allocated based on normal weekly earnings (NWE) starting from the week of the layoff or separation. If the client’s earnings in the last week worked were less than the client’s NWE, the allocation of the vacation pay starts in that week and the earnings last week worked (ELWW) are topped up to NWE with the vacation pay. The remaining vacation pay is then allocated to consecutive weeks based on NWE until it runs out. If the client has received other separation monies, these are combined with the vacation pay and the total of the monies are allocated based on NWE. Note Note Vacation pay that is paid for a specific vacation period In some cases, when clients take a vacation period, they receive compensation for that time. Sometimes, vacation pay for a specific vacation period coincides with another circumstance, such as a separation from the employment or an anniversary date. For the vacation pay to be allocated to the specific vacation period, the following 3 requirements must be met: The vacation period must be scheduled by agreement between the employer and the employee. This can be a written or verbal agreement. A cancelled vacation period no longer fills this requirement. If it is a future vacation period, that future vacation period must be scheduled before the payment of the vacation pay. The clients must be entitled to a vacation period for which they are entitled to pay. Sometimes, contracts list the vacation pay and the vacation period as 2 different entities, not connected in any way. It is not required that the client be paid at the same time leave is taken. The client must be considered employed while taking the leave. When vacation pay is paid out for a specific vacation period, the vacation pay is allocated to the period of the vacation based on the client’s NWE. Allocation starts on the first week of the vacation period and ends on the last week of the vacation period. In cases where the amount of vacation pay is greater than the NWE multiplied by the number of weeks in the vacation period, the balance of vacation pay is not allocated. The allocation still ends with the final week of the vacation period. Vacation pay that is paid on an anniversary date In some cases, vacation pay is paid at a specific time each year, regardless of whether vacation time is taken. This type of vacation pay is considered to be paid on an anniversary date. The allocation starts on the week of the anniversary date and is based on NWE. Other earnings are not taken into account when allocating vacation pay that is payable due to an anniversary date. Vacation pay that is paid at the client’s request Clients may request that their vacation pay be paid out in part or entirely at any given time. The allocation starts on the week the client requested the vacation pay and is based on NWE, regardless of when the employer actually pays the vacation pay. Other earnings are not considered when allocating vacation pay that is payable at the client’s request. Vacation pay amount paid with each pay An employer may decide to include a vacation pay amount with each pay. Vacation pay, paid as a percentage and at the same time as the wages or salary, is allocated to the weeks it is earned and is considered to be part of the client’s NWE. Clients should declare this vacation pay on their claimant’s report together with their salary for the week. At the time of separation, an employer may input a vacation pay amount in block 17A on the ROE. Because the vacation pay amount has been paid with each pay, it must not be allocated as separation monies. The ROE must also be corrected. Note Vacation pay that is paid into a trust fund In some cases, vacation pay is accumulated in a trust fund. The trust fund can be administered by the employer, a union or a third party. The vacation pay is considered earnings at the time it is paid into the trust fund (usually in each pay period), not when it is paid out of the trust fund. When the client chooses to access the vacation pay from the trust fund, it is considered to be savings rather than earnings if the following 3 conditions are met: The monies in the trust fund must be set aside and kept separate from the employer’s control and operations. The employer must set aside the vacation pay each pay period after deducting income tax, Canada Pension Plan, Quebec Pension Plan and EI premiums. Employees must have access to the vacation pay after it is set aside. The vacation pay must not only be kept separate but the employer must also show the steps that have been taken to ensure these funds cannot be accessed by the employer for running the business. Simply placing the funds in a separate bank account is insufficient unless measures, such as having a signed deed in place, exist to ensure the funds can be used only to pay out the vacation savings to the employees. The fund or account in which the monies are held must be used only for the vacation pay, and the employer cannot benefit in any way from the monies deposited into the fund. For the monies to be considered savings, only the employees can benefit from the vacation pay. The monies must be traceable: There must be documents showing the process of depositing the monies to the account and paying out the monies to the employee. If these conditions are met, the vacation pay is not considered earnings at the time it is paid out and is not allocated. If the conditions are not met, the vacation pay is considered earnings and must be allocated accordingly. Labour standard legislation in some provinces specifies that vacation pay accruing to an employee is deemed to be held in trust by the employer. The existence of such legislation is not enough to determine that the vacation pay is paid into a trust fund for the employees. Most vacation pay that is banked by the employer falls into the category of vacation pay held in trust, not vacation pay paid into a trust fund.

During processing, an initial claim displays one of the following statuses: In Progress (Automation) In Progress (Manual) Pending Finalized Finalized Recalculation - In Progress (Automation) Recalculation - In Progress (Manual) Finalized - Pending LREM The Claim action status determines the actions that must be taken to process an allowed antedate. It is not possible to input an antedated BPC when the Claim action status is one of the following: In Progress (Automation) Recalculation - In Progress (Automation) Finalized - Pending LREM Antedate requests are submitted separately from applications for benefits, and there is no way to advise ACP that an antedate has been submitted. As a result, an antedate request has no impact on automation. If all other factors for automation are present, the claim automates regardless of whether there is an antedate request on file. If the claim is automated, it is calculated without the antedate and a recalculation is required. If the claim is in automation and an antedate is allowed, the officer creates a Reminder (REM) WI to request that an employee at National Headquarters remove the claim from the ACP wait process. If the claim is not in automation and the Claim action status is In Progress (Manual) or Recalculation - In Progress (Manual) , an antedate can be input in SSO when the claim is calculated manually so that the claim is established with the antedated BPC.

In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB) (including the EI ERB) was introduced to provide temporary income support to workers without employment or self-employment (SE) earnings due to the pandemic. The EI ERB was available from March 15, 2020 (w/c 2230) to October 3, 2020 (w/c 2258). Clients were eligible for a maximum of 28 weeks and the benefit rate was $500 per week. When a client was entitled to the family supplement (FS), the FS amount was added to the $500.
