A client may attempt to get a refund when tax is deducted on non-taxable amounts or when amounts are taxed at a higher rate than required by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). Refunds are only issued for current tax year. Previous year amounts would have been automatically adjusted by CRA when the client filed their income tax for the year in question. Situations in which a client can be refunded The over-deduction of tax can be refunded to a client only in the following situations: The over-deduction of tax was the result of a Commission error. A client’s request to amend the tax credit code was not actioned in a timely manner and the amount in question was taxed at a higher rate than it should have been. Tax was deducted from a DARS manual payment due to the input of an Account Adjustment (DE020) transaction on an overpayment account where only payments were applied (e.g. TC50 type 140 - Payment received/Adjustment , TC50 type 150 - RCT Set-Off ). Tax was deducted from a PSCD credit refund due to the input of an Adjust Debt t ransaction on an overpayment where only payments were applied. Situations in which a client cannot be refunded The over-deduction of tax cannot be refunded in the following situations: The amounts paid are taxable and the correct tax credit code was applied. Tax was deducted from a DARS manual payment due to the input of a DE020 transaction on an overpayment account from which monies were recouped from EI benefits (e.g. TC50 type 120 - EI Recoupment - CPS , TC50 type 121 - EI Recoupment - MPS or TC50 type 122 - EI Recoupment - BRAC ). Tax was deducted from a PSCD credit refund due to the input of an Adjust Debt transaction on an overpayment from which monies were recouped from EI benefits. Obtaining IPOS authorization IPOS must authorize all requests for tax reimbursement and determines approval on a case-by-case basis. IPOS Amending the tax credit When amending the tax credit on an MPS, blocked or archived claim, the IPOC officer: creates or updates the MPS e-ledger, where applicable; inputs a Master Record (T074) transaction; inputs a Claimant’s Reports (T072) transaction; modifies the Pay History Modification (PHM1) transaction; inputs a Tax File Adjustment (T070) transaction.

Refunds are only issued for current tax year. Previous year amounts would have been automatically adjusted by CRA when the client filed their income tax for the year in question. Situations in which a tax over-deduction can be refunded The over-deduction of tax can be refunded to a client only in the following situations: The over-deduction of tax was the result of a Commission error. A client’s request to amend the tax credit code was not actioned in a timely manner and the amount in question was taxed at a higher rate than it should have been. Tax was deducted from a DARS manual payment due to the input of an Account Adjustment (DE020) transaction on an overpayment account where only payments were applied (e.g. TC50 type 140 - Payment received/Adjustment , TC50 type 150 - RCT Set-Off ). Tax was deducted from a PSCD credit refund due to the input of an Adjust Debt transaction on an overpayment where only payments were applied. Situations in which a tax over-deduction cannot be refunded The over-deduction of tax cannot be refunded in the following situations: The amounts paid are taxable and the correct tax credit code was applied. Tax was deducted from a DARS manual payment due to the input of a DE020 transaction on an overpayment account from which monies were recouped from EI benefits (e.g. TC50 type 120 - EI Recoupment - CPS , TC50 type 121 - EI Recoupment - MPS or TC50 type 122 - EI Recoupment - BRAC ). Tax was deducted from a PSCD credit refund due to the input of an Adjust Debt transaction on an overpayment from which monies were recouped from EI benefits. Note

EIA 25 As of August 5, 2018, a Level 2 officer has the authority to refer clients to self-funded full-time training under EIA 25, as long as the client is identified as a long-tenured worker and all entitlement conditions are met (including contentious issues related to a reason for separation [RFS]). To be considered a long-tenured worker, a client must meet the following 2 conditions: have paid at least 30% of the maximum EI premiums for at least 7 of the last 10 years; not have received more than 35 weeks of regular benefits in the last 156 weeks (3 years) before the BPC of the current claim. The system determines the client’s status when the Initial Intake (M149) transaction is input. When the system is unable to determine the client’s status or if the client disagrees with their status, the officer refers to Determining if a client is a long-tenured worker for more information. Determining if a client is a long-tenured worker If a client was initially categorized as a long-tenured worker before the claim was established (when the Initial Decision [M103] transaction was processed) and the status changes after the course is approved (e.g. the client has not paid sufficient premiums during the last 7 out of 10 years), Service Canada does not reverse the decision. The officer documents the information on a record of decision (ROD). If there is a subsequent claim and the client is attending the same full-time training, the long-tenured worker criteria are not re-evaluated on the subsequent claim. The client is still considered a long-tenured worker. The officer creates a ROD confirming that the client was categorized as a long-tenured worker for a previous BPC. If there is a subsequent claim and the client is attending a new full-time training, the long-tenured worker criteria must be evaluated on the subsequent claim.

If the Level 1 officer cannot adjudicate the issue, the WI is referred to Level 2 for adjudication. When an ADJ WI is created on a renewal claim, either manually or by the system, the system automatically imposes a 2 - Contentious renewal in automation manual action (MA02) to prevent payment of benefits until the contentious issue is adjudicated and the renewal is complete. When the ADJ WI is completed, the system removes the MA02. An officer cannot remove an MA02. The Level 1 officer who refers the file to Level 2 for adjudication must: initiate fact-finding; input the conversion; reassign the WI. When opening an ADJ WI, the officer must always verify if there is a Resolve Issue tab. If there is a Resolve Issue tab, the officer documents the decision directly in the ADJ WI by completing all mandatory screens. When the ADJ WI is completed, NWS creates a record of decision (ROD) based on the Resolve Issue screens. When the renewal is finalized, the system also generates the required transactions (e.g. signature code, disentitlement) based on the Resolve Issue screens. If a disentitlement or indefinite disqualification is imposed, the system creates a Correspondence (COR) WI for the D-01-00-00 letter. This means that the officer with the CA or SA WI has no action to perform for these ADJ WIs. If there is no Resolve Issue tab for the ADJ WI, the officer with the ADJ WI creates a ROD, generates the required transactions and sends the appropriate letter. If there is an outstanding CA or SA WI when the officer completes the ADJ WI, a client Note is created and the officer with the CA or SA WI follows the instructions to input the transactions or send the letter.

To notify Integrity that a client’s claim is blocked due to an MA71, or that a suspicious ROE was used in the initial calculation, the officer creates an urgent AI WI so that the investigation can be prioritized.

Many fraudulent applications have been submitted with suspicious ROEs and could have been used to calculate a client’s claim. The following are some indicators that an ROE may be suspicious: The employer name or occupation on the ROE does not match other ROEs in RCM (e.g. the client’s employment history is with the School District 123, but an ROE is received from a plumbing company). The employer name on the ROE does not match the employment information provided by the client on previous applications. The employer name on the ROE does not match the last employer on the initial application. The employer name indicated as the last employer on the initial application is a large well-known corporation, but the name indicated on the ROE (block 4 - Employer’s name ) is a person’s name (e.g. the last employer on the application is Wal-Mart, but the employer on the ROE is John Doe). The ROE is a paper ROE issued by a large company that normally issues electronic ROEs (or vice versa).

On March 15, 2020, the Government of Canada introduced the EI Emergency Response Benefit (EI ERB) to provide temporary income support to workers impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic. In the weeks that followed, it was discovered that the personal information of many Canadians was used to fraudulently establish EI ERB claims, EI claims and to renew non-fraudulent claims. The Level 2 officers who are part of the specialized team follow this procedure when a claim has been renewed by a third party and payments have been issued on a blocked claim. When an Integrity investigator sends the case for action, the Integrity investigator creates a CR Integrity ERB-EI Transition WI. Note When a third party has used the client’s personal information to renew a claim after a client either returned to work or stopped completing claimant’s reports, a processing officer inputs the required transactions to correct the file and the IPOC officer removes the payments from the client’s file. Fraudulent activity in EI applications is discovered in several different ways, including the following: The client receives a T4E without having applied for benefits and contacts the call centre. A returned payment raises suspicion about a bank account. A client’s claim is transferred to another ITC and the client can no longer complete claimant’s reports. A client files a new application and an officer discovers fraud indicators on a previous application while processing the claim. fraud indicators A client files a new application and a renewal is completed instead of a new claim because there is an existing fraudulent BPC. A client has an existing claim and a third party renews the client’s claim. The renewal results in the client’s banking information being changed to a bank account not owned by the client. A third party modifies the client’s banking information. The client or third party completes claimant’s reports, which results in misdirected payments. A fraudulent ROE was issued in a fraudulent EI application submitted by a third party. The address and banking information provided by the third party must be updated to the client’s information, even if the client is not requesting benefits. In FTS, ensure that the address and banking information are updated and that the client’s name, language and gender are correct. If there is a fraudulent claim in another ITC, update the client’s information in both ITCs. When processing a Level 2 CR Integrity - ERB-EI Transition WI, it is possible that some transactions related to the fraudulent application may have already been enteredinput into the file. The officer should still continue with the procedure to ensure that all required actions have been taken.

When an EI payment is not received, or is lost, stolen, destroyed or stale-dated, a payment replacement can be issued to the client. Before requesting that IPOC process a payment replacement, the officer reviews the file. A payment replacement can be requested when: the address on file is accurate; the name of the client is the same as the one indicated on the original payment; the client is entitled to the same amount as the original payment; the payment replacement corresponds to the same weeks as the original payment; the payment status in SPS is not Cancelled . If any of the above conditions do not apply, the IPOC officer must remove the original payment from the client’s file and issue a new payment in MPS.

The Level 2 officer must consult NIIS for each case to find all the relevant information to review the issue. After conducting a full review of the investigation, if the Level 2 officer determines that facts are missing, the officer returns the file to Integrity for further fact-finding. The officer indicates the information that is missing but necessary to adjudicate the issue. The Level 2 officer does not adjudicate the issue if facts are missing or incomplete. Missing or incomplete information could include: the client’s current address information; the client’s current banking information; whether the client is requesting benefits or not; the renewal week, if the client is requesting benefits; the claimant’s report information, if the client is requesting benefits; whether payments have been issued to the client or the third party; fraudulent ROEs to be deleted or that have been deleted from the client’s file. Note The officer ensures that the investigator has also included information about any related contentious issues, if necessary. For more information on navigating NIIS, the officer refers to the National Integrity Investigation System (NIIS) User Reference Guide . A reconsideration under EIA 112 can be held in abeyance in the following 4 situations: EIA 112 BPNE pending an appeal of an earlier decision Earlier decisions such as voluntary leaving, misconduct or violation can affect whether a benefit period can be established. The appeal of the earlier decision must be resolved before the reconsideration under EIA 112 of the BPNE can be performed. EIA 112 Waiting for instruction from National Headquarters National Headquarters may instruct agents to hold certain files in abeyance pending a decision from a higher court or a decision on the application of a new policy. Labour disputes, railway misconduct cases, major fraud investigations or other complex files There may be situations that involve local or regional discussions with the union involved in a labour dispute or railway misconduct, or that involve major fraud investigations leading to numerous requests for reconsideration. There may also be other complex files involving one or many clients. In such situations, the agent determines whether the reconsideration must be held in abeyance. If unsure of the decision to be made, the agent can consult a business expertise advisor. Insurability The client requests the review of a decision (e.g. BPNE), questions the insurable hours or earnings of an employment and there is no Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) insurability ruling on file, or there is an insurability ruling but the client provides new facts that the CRA must assess. The client is waiting for an insurability ruling from the CRA, a decision from the Minister of National Revenue (an appeal of a CRA ruling) or from the Tax Court of Canada (an appeal of a decision of the Minister of National Revenue). The reconsideration under EIA 112 is held in abeyance until decision is made by the CRA, Minister of National Revenue or Tax Court of Canada. Note Note Example Before the file can be held in abeyance a written proof is required when the client is waiting for a decision in any of the following circumstances: The client has submitted his or her own request to the CRA for an insurability ruling. The client has submitted a request for a decision to the Minister of National Revenue. The client has submitted a request for a decision to the Tax Court of Canada, as a CRA decision has been further appealed. The proof includes, but is not limited to: a copy of the request for an insurability ruling; a letter confirming receipt of a request for an insurability ruling; a letter confirming receipt of an appeal to the Minister of National Revenue; or a letter confirming receipt of an appeal to the Tax Court of Canada.

On March 15, 2020, the Government of Canada introduced the EI Emergency Response Benefit (EI ERB) to provide temporary income support to workers impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic. In the weeks that followed, it was discovered that the personal information of many Canadians was used to fraudulently establish EI ERB claims or EI claims. The discovery of fraudulent activity in EI applications occurs in several different ways, including the following: The client receives a T4E without having applied for benefits and contacts the call centre. A returned payment raises suspicions about a bank account. A client’s claim is transferred to another information technology centre (ITC) and the client can no longer complete claimant’s reports. A client files a new application and an officer discovers fraud indicators on a previous application while processing the claim. fraud indicators A client files a new EI application and a renewal is completed instead of a new claim because there is an existing fraudulent BPC. A client has an existing claim and a third party renews the client’s claim. The renewal results in the client’s banking information being changed to a bank account not owned by the client. A third party modifies the client’s banking information. The client or third party completes claimant’s reports, which results in misdirected payments. A fraudulent ROE was issued in a fraudulent EI application submitted by a third party.

The Level 1 officer can review a fraudulent claim related to the client’s continuing claim in the following situations: The Level 1 officer receives an AI WI and all of the following conditions are met: no payment has been issued to the client or third party on the fraudulent claim (this includes any payment that was issued and later updated to Cancelled or Returned in SPS) ; the third party is unknown; no potentially fraudulent ROEs were used to calculate the client’s claim for the same BPC. The Level 1 officer receives a CR Integrity - ERB-EI Transition WI and all of the following conditions are met: no payment was issued to the third party on the fraudulent claim (this includes any payment that was issued and later updated to Cancelled or Returned in SPS) ; the third party is unknown; no other contentious issues requiring a Level 2 decision were reported in the investigation or in another investigation for the same BPC. The Level 1 officer receives an AI WI and a CR Integrity - ERB-EI Transition WI and all of the following conditions are met: no payment was issued to the third party on the fraudulent claim (this includes any payment that was issued and later updated to Cancelled or Returned in SPS) ; the third party is unknown; no other contentious issues requiring a Level 2 decision were reported in the investigation or in another investigation for the same BPC. When the conditions above are not met, the Level 1 officer does the following: If there is only an AI WI, the Level 1 officer reassigns it to Integrity. If there is only a CR Integrity - ERB-EI Transition WI, the Level 1 officer reassigns it to Level 2. If there is an AI WI and a CR Integrity - ERB-EI Transition WI, the Level 1 officer completes the AI WI and reassigns the CR WI to Level 2.

Once a client has established a benefit period (BP), benefits may be paid for any week of unemployment when the client meets the entitlement provisions to receive benefits. A week of unemployment is any week in which a client works less than a full working week and has less than a full week’s wages. Generally, a client is considered to have worked a full working week and is not entitled to EI benefits during any week if the client meets one of the following: is self-employed is engaged in the operation of a business (including farming) on the client’s own account or in a partnership or co-adventure is employed in any other employment in which the client controls their working hours However, under certain circumstances a client engaged in SE or the operation of a farm may be considered to be unemployed and not working a full work week. This occurs when the client can show that their work in SE or the operation of the farm, during the period for which they are claiming benefits, is to such a minor extent that a person could not be normally rely on that SE or farm as their principal means of earning a living. Whenever a client reports farming activities or earnings, the extent of the client’s involvement must be reviewed to determine entitlement to benefits. There are 6 factors to consider in determining whether the client is engaged in SE activities or operation of a farm to such a minor extent that a person would not rely on that employment as a principal means of livelihood: time spent on the SE or farming activities nature and amount of the capital and resources invested financial success or failure of the employment or business continuity of the employment or business nature of the employment or business client's intention and willingness to seek and immediately accept alternate employment Farming differs from other SE when it is determined that the client is engaged in farming as a principal means of livelihood and a not unemployed disentitlement applies. Special consideration is given to the period from the week of October 1 to the week of March 31, as stated in Regulation 30(4) . The client may be entitled to benefits during this regulatory off-season if the farming activity is so minor in extent that the client is not prevented from accepting full-time employment. Earnings from farming during this period are allocated. Regulation 30(4) The period defined in Regulation 30(4) cannot be modified or extended to match the client’s situation. Regulation 30(4) When it is determined that the client is self-employed in farming and their involvement is not minor in extent, the client is considered to be working full work weeks (i.e. not unemployed) and EI benefits are not payable. A 1 - Not unemployed disentitlement (D1) is imposed. A D1 is imposed for full weeks of disentitlement only and is applicable to all benefit types. Partial weeks of disentitlement at the beginning or end of a period of being not unemployed are added to claims for regular or fishing benefits using a 3 - Not available disentitlement (D3). Partial weeks of disentitlement do not apply to special benefits, but the SE (farming) earnings are allocated. Refer to the Earnings procedure. Earnings Note

EI is designed to provide temporary benefits to those who are unemployed. Persons engaged in the operation of a farm are considered to be self-employed in farming. This self-employment (SE) must be adjudicated to determine if the client is entitled to EI while engaged in the farming activities. Farm operators are non-salaried persons whose occupational activity consists of working on a farm. They may look after all operations, such as the production, distribution and marketing of farm products, with the intent to realize a profit. Their activities may also include the maintenance of buildings, equipment and fences. Farming includes activities such as: cultivation of the soil to produce field-grown crops horticulture apiculture poultry farming maple production aquaculture pisciculture wood from farm woodlots raising or breeding animals useful to mankind dairy farming tobacco production production of wool, fibre and fodder plants Note Renting land for the purpose of farming There is a difference between farming and the rental of land only. Persons who are not engaged in farming on their own behalf but who rent land to others to be used for farming activities are not considered self-employed in farming. The rental of land only is not considered farming.

Once a client has established a benefit period (BP), benefits may be paid for any week of unemployment when the client meets the entitlement provisions to receive benefits. A week of unemployment is any week in which a client works less than a full work week (FWW) and has less than a full week’s earnings. Generally, a client is considered to have worked a FWW and is not entitled to EI benefits during any week if the client meets one of the following: is self-employed; is engaged in the operation of a business (including farming) on the client’s own account or in a partnership or co-adventure; is employed in any other employment in which the client controls their working hours. However, under certain circumstances a client engaged in SE or the operation of a business may be considered to be unemployed and not working a FWW. This occurs when the client can show that their work in SE or the operation of the business, during the period for which they are claiming benefits is to such a minor extent that a person could not normally rely on that employment or business as their principal means of earning a living. Whenever a client reports SE activities (including farming) or earnings, the extent of the client’s involvement must be reviewed to determine entitlement to benefits. There are 6 factors to consider in determining whether the client is employed or engaged in the operation of a business to such a minor extent that a person would not rely on that employment or engagement as a principal means of livelihood: time spent on the SE; nature and amount of the capital and resources invested; financial success or failure of the employment or business; continuity of the employment or business; nature of the employment or business; client's intention and willingness to seek and immediately accept alternate employment. When a client quits, retires or is dismissed due to SE, it may indicate that the SE is not minor in extent and must be adjudicated at Level 2. When it is determined that the client is engaged in SE and their involvement is not minor in extent, a client is considered to be working FWWs (i.e. not unemployed) and EI benefits are not payable. A 1 - Not unemployed disentitlement (D1) is imposed. A D1 is imposed for full weeks of disentitlement only and applies to all benefit types (BTs). Partial weeks of disentitlement at the beginning or end of a period of being not unemployed are added to claims for regular or fishing benefits using a 3 - Not available disentitlement (D3). Partial weeks of disentitlement do not apply to special benefits, but the SE earnings are allocated. Refer to the Earnings procedure. Earnings Note

EI is designed to provide temporary benefits to those who are unemployed. If the client only demonstrates a natural concern for his investment, he is not considered self-employed.

Envelopes containing a benefit statement can be distinguished from other envelopes by a 4-digit Responsibility Centre code displayed in the top left of the address window. If the undeliverable mail is a benefit statement, it may contain an access code. When the benefit statement also contains an access code, only the letter P is displayed after the Responsibility Centre code. The letters NP mean there is no access code in the envelope. Example The officer does not open the envelope containing the benefit statement and access code since the officer must not see the client’s full access code. If a benefit statement is returned as undeliverable, the officer creates an SROC detailing the undeliverable mail, and the envelope may need to be imaged. Note

A 23 - Teacher - Non-teaching period (D23) disentitlement may be imposed on a client applying for regular or sickness benefits during the non-teaching periods if the following 2 situations apply: the client was employed in teaching for any part of the QP; the client is under a teaching contract during the BP. Annex 2 in Digest 14 — Teachers provides a decision chart for casual or substitute teachers. Please refer to it to determine if a D23 must be imposed. Annex 2 Digest 14 — Teachers The officer adjudicates entitlement to benefits for all non-teaching periods. If entitlement is not proven, a D23 is imposed for all non-teaching periods in the BP. The BE 2022-02 — Teachers: Disentitlement for the Non-Teaching Periods provides the guidance for imposing disentitlements for all non-teaching periods. BE 2022-02 — Teachers: Disentitlement for the Non-Teaching Periods The officer creates one record of decision (ROD) including all non-teaching periods in the BP for which a D23 was imposed. The officer sends a notice of decision letter including all non-teaching periods in the BP for which a D23 was imposed. The officer is no longer required to follow up on subsequent non-teaching periods. When a teacher files a claim for benefits, the officer adjudicates the entitlement for all non-teaching periods in the BP and includes each period of the D23 in the notice of decision letter. Therefore, a Reminder (REM) WI is not created.

When a teacher was under contract in a teaching employment and has accumulated hours of insurable employment during the QP, no regular benefits can be paid for any of the weeks that fall in a non-teaching period if the client is under contract during the BP and there are linkages between the contracts. There are 3 exceptions to this rule that allow a teacher to receive regular benefits during the non-teaching period: The contract of employment for teaching has terminated. All employment in teaching is on a casual or substitute basis. The client qualifies to receive benefits based on employment in an occupation other than teaching. If none of these exceptions applies, the teacher is disentitled from benefits during the non-teaching period(s). Termination of a contract A teacher whose contract of employment for teaching has terminated may receive benefits during any non-teaching period. To determine if the contract has terminated, consider these 2 factors: Has the teacher received a new contract or a verbal agreement before the end of the current contract? Do linkages exist between the contracts? To determine if linkages exist between the contracts, the teacher must answer the following questions: Is the teacher’s seniority carried forward from one contract year to the next? Are pension contributions carried forward from one contract to the next? Are accumulated sick leave credits carried forward from one contract to the next? Is the teacher entitled to benefits during the summer? If so, what types of benefits (disability, life, dental, medical, etc.)? Who pays the premiums during the summer? Casual or substitute teaching To meet the exception set out in EIR 33(2)(b) , any employment in teaching during the QP must be on a casual or substitute basis. EIR 33(2)(b) If the contract for substitute teaching becomes fixed or regular or subject to a temporary contract, regardless of the terms and conditions of the teaching contract, the employment can no longer be considered casual or substitute. Occupation other than teaching during the qualifying period (QP) The EIR sets out an exemption allowing a teacher who meets the qualifying conditions to have a BP established using ROEs for employment other than teaching. In this situation, Level 2 officers must exclude the ROEs for teaching employment, clearly indicate their decision in a ROD and create a REM WI for Level 1 to monitor the calculation of the claim. Level 1 officers verify that the claim is established correctly and recalculate the claim, if necessary. Refer to the appropriate Calculation or Recalculation procedure. When applying for EI benefits, clients are asked if they are part of a group of employees in an apprenticeship program and if they were given a reference code to submit their application. If they answer yes, they are prompted to enter the 16-digit code. When they enter the reference code, a specialized EI application is presented. If they answer no, they are presented with a regular EI application. The reference code contains the following information: Service Canada Processing Centre (digits 1 to 4) Apprenticeship application form type (02) (digits 5 and 6) Year (digits 7 to 10) Identifier (digits 11 to 16) Clients may indicate on the EI application that they do not have a reference code, but later indicate that they are an apprentice and attending a full-time course of instruction to which they were referred by a designated authority. In this situation, clients must provide proof of the referral to the apprenticeship course. As proof, clients may provide one of the following: the reference code they were given a copy of the training documentation given to them by the provincial program officer when they registered for the course. If clients provide proof of the referral to the apprenticeship course, the system uses the reference code provided to create a partial Project Data - Training (M171) transaction when the claim is calculated. If clients do not provide proof of the referral, the client’s attendance at the course of instruction must be adjudicated as non-referred training. The reference code serves only as proof of referral to the course, and clients are considered available for work while attending the course. The reference code does not authorize clients to quit their employment to attend the approved training course. A contentious reason for separation (RFS) requires adjudication.

Clients can be referred to training by the province or territory through a labour market development agreement, a labour market agreement for persons with disabilities or a Canada Job Fund agreement. Available referred training options vary by province or territory based on these agreements, but they include the following programs: Literacy and essential skills training (adult learning) Canada Job Grant Job Creation Partnerships Self-employment benefits Additionally, in all regions, a client can be referred to training by the Indigenous Skills and Employment Training Program. Western Canada and Territories region In the Western Canada and Territories region, a client can be referred to training through: the Ministry of Jobs, Tourism and Skills Training (Labour), through WorkBC (British Columbia) the Ministry of Jobs, Skills, Training and Labour, through Alberta Works (Alberta) the Ministry of the Economy, through Canada-Saskatchewan Labour Market Services (Saskatchewan) Manitoba Jobs and Economy, through Employment Manitoba (Manitoba) the Department of Education, through Employment Assistance Service Providers (Yukon) the Department of Education, Culture and Employment, through ECE Service Centre (Northwest Territories) the Department of Family Services (Nunavut) Ontario region In the Ontario region, a client can be referred to training through: the Ministry of Labour, Immigration, Training and Skills Development, through Employment Ontario’s network of service providers Quebec region In the Quebec region, a client can be referred to training through: the Ministry of Labour, Employment and Social Solidarity, through Centre local d’emploi Atlantic region In the Atlantic region, a client can be referred to training through: the Ministry of Innovation and Advanced Learning, through SkillsPEI (Prince Edward Island) the Ministry of Labour and Advanced Education, through Employment Nova Scotia (Nova Scotia) the Department of Advanced Education and Skills (Newfoundland and Labrador) the Ministry of Post-Secondary Education, Training and Labour, through Employment and Continuous Learnings Services (New Brunswick) Long-tenured workers A client who reports attending full-time training may be identified as a long-tenured worker. If the conditions are met, a client who is identified as a long-tenured worker and who wishes to attend self-funded full-time training can be referred to that training by Service Canada. To be considered a long-tenured worker, a client must meet the following 2 conditions: have paid at least 30% of the maximum EI premiums for at least 7 of the last 10 years; not have received more than 35 weeks of regular benefits in the last 156 weeks (3 years) before the BPC of the current claim. Service Canada has the authority to approve full-time training for a long-tenured worker. However, before adjudicating training, the officer adjudicates other contentious issues to determine if the client is entitled to benefits. This can help the client better understand the decision-making process, as the client may assume that for a referred training situation, contentious issues are automatically allowed. When a client is identified as a long-tenured worker, the officer refers to Adjudicating training for a long-tenured worker — Continuing claim . When clients report that they are attending full-time training on their own initiative, the officer refers to BE 2023-05 — Federal Court of Appeal decision: William Page (A-29-22) and availability for students on full-time training and the Digest of Benefit Entitlement Principles 10.12.2.8 — Hours of work . Both the BE Memo and the Digest explain that, under FCA A-29-22 , when adjudicating availability, the officer must consider the clients’ work history while attending training, in addition to other factors (i.e. the number of hours clients are attending training). Clients can rebut the presumption of non-availability if they can demonstrate having a regular work history outside of the training hours while taking full-time training. Using any previous ROEs, the officer reviews the number of hours the client worked while attending training to determine if the client can rebut the presumption of non-availability. Clients must also demonstrate a willingness and ability to remain available for a similar work schedule. Clients must not reduce or restrict their available hours of work beyond what is reasonable, given their work history, while attending training. BE 2023-05 — Federal Court of Appeal decision: William Page (A-29-22) and availability for students on full-time training Digest of Benefit Entitlement Principles 10.12.2.8 — Hours of work FCA A-29-22 The officer determines the total number of hours per week that is being spent on the training, including : class time study time time spent working on assignments time spent doing research Additional fact-finding or follow-up is not required when a client reports training of up to 9 hours per week. Clients attending a training course equal to or greater than 10 hours per week must be willing to seek and accept all hours of work that are available to them in the labour market, including evenings, nights, shift work, inconvenient or long hours and overtime. A client who is unwilling or unable to quit the course in order to accept these hours of work, or whose job search efforts demonstrate such an unwillingness or inability, may not be able to prove availability for work. The client’s individual circumstances must be examined to determine if the client is avoiding suitable employment because of an unwillingness or inability to work certain hours. If so, a disentitlement may be imposed. Correspondence courses are treated the same as any other training.

Taking a training course on one’s own initiative creates an availability issue. When clients are receiving regular benefits, they must be available for and actively seeking employment. Training should not limit a client’s employment opportunities. A client receiving fishing benefits may also take training. The adjudication and inputs are the same whether the claim is for regular or fishing benefits. This includes clients who are attending short-term training courses and targeted initiatives. For a complete list of non-referred short-term courses and targeted initiatives, the officer refers to the job aid . job aid Before adjudicating availability during non-referred training, it is important to first consider whether the client could be referred to the course under EIA 25 . This step ensures that entitlement to benefits is correctly determined. Clients are considered unemployed and capable of and available for work when attending referred training. EIA 25 Note Long-tenured workers A client who reports attending full-time training may be identified as a long-tenured worker. If the conditions are met, a client who is identified as a long-tenured worker and who wishes to attend self-funded full-time training can be referred to that training by Service Canada. To be considered a long-tenured worker, a client must meet the following 2 conditions: have paid at least 30% of the maximum EI premiums for at least 7 of the last 10 years; not have received more than 35 weeks of regular benefits in the last 156 weeks (3 years) before the BPC of the current claim. Service Canada has the authority to approve full-time training for a long-tenured worker. However, before adjudicating training, the officer adjudicates other contentious issues to determine if the client is entitled to benefits. This can help the client better understand the decision-making process, as the client may assume that for a referred training situation, contentious issues are automatically allowed. When a client is identified as a long-tenured worker, the officer refers to Adjudicating training for a long-tenured worker — Continuing claim . Adjudicating training for a long-tenured worker — Continuing claim Note

Additional fact-finding or follow-up is not required when a client reports training of up to 9 hours per week. When training is equal to or greater than 10 hours, but less than 15 hours per week, it must be determined that if not for the medical situation, the client would be available and capable of working, and that upon recovery, the intention is to look for full-time work. The client must also be willing to quit the course to accept full-time employment once recovered from the illness or injury. When clients report that they are attending full-time training on their own initiative, the officer refers to BE 2023-05 — Federal Court of Appeal decision: William Page (A-29-22) and availability for students on full-time training and the Digest of Benefit Entitlement Principles 10.12.2.8 — Hours of work . Both the BE Memo and the Digest explain that, under FCA A-29-22 , when adjudicating availability, the officer must consider the clients’ work history while attending training, in addition to other factors (i.e. the number of hours clients are attending training). Clients can rebut the presumption of non-availability if they can demonstrate having a regular work history outside of the training hours while taking full-time training. Using any previous ROEs, the officer reviews the number of hours the client worked while attending training to determine if the client can rebut the presumption of non-availability. Clients must also demonstrate a willingness and ability to remain available for a similar work schedule. Clients must not reduce or restrict their available hours of work beyond what is reasonable, given their work history, while attending training. BE 2023-05 — Federal Court of Appeal decision: William Page (A-29-22) and availability for students on full-time training Digest of Benefit Entitlement Principles 10.12.2.8 — Hours of work FCA A-29-22 When a client is devoting 15 or more hours per week to training, the agent must determine the total number of hours per week that is being spent on the training, including : class time study time time spent working on assignments time spent doing research Correspondence courses are treated the same as any other training, with the following conditions applied: the course obligations must be outside the client’s normal working hours; upon recovery, the client must be willing to quit the course to accept full-time employment; upon recovery, the client must not limit the acceptance of full-time employment in favour of the training.

Each region has specific procedures in place for submitting the document authorizing the client to quit their employment. In some regions, the client is responsible for submitting a copy to Service Canada. In other regions, the designated authority submits it directly to Service Canada. When the information is not on file, the officer fact-finds to complete the WI related to the voluntary leaving. When clients state that they have been authorized to quit, but a copy of the authorization is not on file, the officer advises the clients to ask the designated authority to provide it. If the authorization is not submitted, the officer adjudicates the voluntary leaving based on the information on file. Agreements with the provinces, territories and indigenous groups exist for implementing programs that are similar to Service Canada’s employment programs. These include: Labour Market Development Agreements for training-related employment measures managed by the provinces and territories. Indigenous Skills and Employment Training Program for training-related employment measures managed by various indigenous groups for indigenous individuals. Sometimes an unemployed client is referred to training that starts at a future date and the client becomes employed before the training begins. If the client leaves this employment to attend the training, the issue is referred to Level 2 since the voluntary leaving has not been recommended or approved by the designated authority.

When clients voluntarily leave their employment, the officer must determine if they had just cause for leaving. Just cause means that when all factors are considered, the client had no reasonable alternative but to leave the employment. If it is determined that the client left the employment without just cause, a disqualification is imposed on the claim for regular benefits, unless there are enough insurable hours since the voluntary leaving to establish a new claim. In this case, the ROE with the voluntary leaving is excluded from the calculation of the claim. The objective of a workforce reduction program is to ensure the economic viability of a company, an organization, a firm or a plant. To remain competitive, employers may have to restructure their workforce, which could include permanently reducing the number of employees. The group covered under a workforce reduction program may be all the employees (including seasonal, temporary or on call employees) or it could be limited to a sector, a particular group of workers or a particular work site. Workforce reduction could also include as little as one employee. Employees who leave under an approved workforce reduction program have a complete severance from their employment. The details of the workforce reduction program must be documented. The appropriate regional workforce reduction coordinator renders all decisions on a workforce reduction program. The regional coordinator ensures that the initial fact-finding is completed and that decisions on workforce reduction programs are made and posted in Major Employer Events . Major Employer Events If a decision has not yet been posted in Major Employer Events , the officer completes the email template and sends it to the regional workforce reduction coordinator for the region where the employer’s head office is located. EIR 51 A workforce reduction program is defined in EIR 51(2) as a program: EIR 51(2) that is initiated by the employer; that has as its objective a permanent reduction in the number of employees; that offers employees the option to leaving employment voluntarily; whose elements are documented by the employer. Employers planning a workforce reduction program may submit a request to Service Canada for confirmation that their plan meets the requirements of the EIR. The request should contain information confirming: the plan was initiated by the employer; the objective is to permanently reduce the workforce; the employees covered by the program. Service Canada cannot provide a blanket decision that applies to all employees, but provides an employer with prior confirmation that an employer’s workforce reduction program meets the conditions of EIR 51 . EIR 51 Regions usually have procedures in place for documenting approved workforce reduction programs. For information about approved workforce reduction programs, the officer refers to Major Employer Events . Employers are often advised to confirm the existence of a valid workforce reduction program in the Comments block of the ROE. If there is no documentation confirming the workforce reduction program as valid, or if the employer has not documented the ROE to that effect, the officer must fact-find with the employer. When the ADJ WI is completed, the system creates a record of decision (ROD) based on the Resolve Issue screens. When the renewal is finalized, the system generates the required transactions based on the Resolve Issue screens and removes the stop payment (MA02). If the previous decision resulted in a ROD created by the system, the system creates a new ROD with the same information when the ADJ WI is completed. If the previous decision resulted in a ROD created manually, the officer indicates the applicable special condition based on the previous decision.

When clients voluntarily leave their employment, the officer must determine if they had just cause for leaving. Just cause means that when all factors are considered, the client had no reasonable alternative but to leave the employment. If it is determined that the client left the employment without just cause, a disqualification is imposed on the claim for regular benefits, unless there are enough insurable hours since the voluntary leaving to establish a new claim. In this case, the ROE with the voluntary leaving is excluded from the calculation of the claim. A designated authority may authorize clients to leave their employment in order to attend referred training or an employment activity under EIA 25 . In that situation, clients have just cause for leaving their employment, provided they do so in the 2 weeks before the start of the program. EIA 25 To confirm that the client has been authorized to leave the employment, the designated authority gives the client an official document sometimes referred to as an authorization to quit or a counsel to leave employment. Note An ROE is not required to adjudicate a voluntary leaving.

When clients voluntarily leave their employment, the officer must determine if they had just cause for leaving. Just cause means that when all factors are considered, the client had no reasonable alternative but to leave the employment. If it is determined that the client left the employment without just cause, a disqualification is imposed on the claim for regular benefits, unless there are enough insurable hours since the voluntary leaving to establish a new claim. In this case, the ROE with the voluntary leaving is excluded from the calculation of the claim. A designated authority may authorize clients to leave their employment in order to attend referred training or an employment activity under EIA 25 . In that situation, clients have just cause for leaving their employment, provided they do so in the 2 weeks before the start of the program. EIA 25 To confirm that the client has been authorized to leave the employment, the designated authority gives the client an official document sometimes referred to as an authorization to quit or a counsel to leave employment. An ROE is not required to adjudicate voluntary leaving. Note

ACP may adjudicate voluntary leaving on an initial claim in the following situations: The client follows a spouse or a common-law partner who is relocating to a new residence. The client follows a fiancé to a new residence. The client moves with a parent or legal guardian to a new residence. If ACP adjudicates a voluntary leaving and the officer identifies a discrepancy (e.g. ACP automates a decision based on the client’s spouse being relocated for work, but fact-finding with the client reveals the spouse relocated for other reasons), the officer must review the information and amend the decision. Note

On renewal claims, ACP may adjudicate if the voluntary leaving is for one of the following reasons: The client follows a spouse or a common-law partner who is relocating to a new residence. The client follows a fiancé(e) to a new residence. The client moves with a parent or legal guardian to a new residence. If ACP adjudicates a voluntary leaving and the officer identifies a discrepancy (e.g. ACP automates a decision based on the client’s spouse being relocated for work, but during fact-finding the client reveals the spouse relocated for other reasons), the officer must review the information and amend the decision.

Note When clients voluntarily leave their employment, the officer must determine if they had just cause for leaving. Just cause means that when all factors are considered, the client had no reasonable alternative but to leave the employment. If it is determined that the client left the employment without just cause, a disqualification is imposed on the claim for regular benefits, unless the client has worked enough insurable hours since the voluntary leaving to establish a new claim. In this case, the ROE with the voluntary leaving is excluded from the calculation of the claim. Medical documentation supporting the voluntary leaving is required to adjudicate the issue at Level 1 ( National Policy on Levels of Decision ). If the client does not provide acceptable medical documentation related to the voluntary leaving, a Level 2 officer must adjudicate the reason for separation (RFS). Medical documentation is accepted from a licensed medical doctor (Canadian or American) or, if the illness being treated is within the practitioner’s field, from the following practitioners: National Policy on Levels of Decision psychologist; chiropractor; optometrist; podiatrist; dentist; registered doctor of traditional Chinese medicine or Registered traditional Chinese medicine practitioner recognized by the province; nurse practitioner; midwife; registered nurse (only in isolated areas when a doctor is not available). An ROE is not required to adjudicate voluntary leaving. In NWS, there may be a “New ROE” message displayed on the Adjudication Issue (ADJ) WI for the voluntary leaving issue. The adjudicating officer gathers all relevant information and completes all fact-finding before adjudicating the issue. The Level 2 officer must: offer the client and the employer the opportunity to provide information concerning the RFS; allow both parties to provide an explanation or clarification when there are contradictory statements; give the client the opportunity to provide a final rebuttal; take this information into account when adjudicating the issue; give the client the benefit of the doubt when the facts provided by the client and those provided by the employer are equally credible. Fact-finding — Voluntary leaving for personal reasons In cases where clients voluntarily leave their employment strictly for personal reasons (e.g. returning to school, changing careers, providing care for an ill child), it is unnecessary to contact the employer again after the initial fact-finding if: the facts are credible; considering all factors, it is unlikely that the employer has any information about the existence or absence of other reasonable alternatives for the client. Client wishes employer not be contacted In cases where the voluntary leaving is not strictly for personal reasons and the client does not want the employer to be contacted, officers must explain that they are legally required to fact-find with the employer. If the client insists that the employer not be contacted, officers advise the client that the only alternative is to withdraw the claim for benefits. Officers document the client’s request to withdraw the claim. Refer to Withdrawing an application . Une antidate peut être sous-entendue ou demandée formellement. Un client qui présente une demande de prestations spéciales plus de 4 semaines après le dernier jour de travail (DJT) doit indiquer la raison de son retard. Un client peut laisser sous-entendre qu’il demande une antidate dans sa réponse à la question dans sa demande d’AE. La réponse d’un client peut être considérée comme une demande d’antidate sans que le client présente une demande formelle d’antidate quand la seule raison du retard est l’ une des suivantes : Le client recevait ou attendait de recevoir des paiements d’un employeur ou d’un autre assureur ou payeur, y compris des indemnités d’incapacité et des indemnités de départ ou de cessation d’emploi. Le client était malade ou blessé et physiquement incapable de remplir la demande. Le client devait fournir des soins ou du soutien à un membre de la famille malade. Le client devait fournir des soins ou du soutien à un patient gravement malade ou blessé. Les antidates sous-entendues surviennent le plus souvent dans les demandes de prestations spéciales parce que la question sur le retard est dans la demande. Dans le cas des demandes pour d’autres GP, si les renseignements au dossier sur le retard correspondent à une des raisons ci-dessus, l’agent les traite de la même façon. Si des renseignements au dossier indiquent que la demande a été présentée en retard pour plus d’une raison ou pour toute autre raison que celles énumérées ci-dessus, elle n’est pas considérée comme une demande d’antidate sous-entendue. Dans ce cas, aucune autre mesure n’est prise concernant le retard, sauf si le client présente une demande d’antidate officielle. Une fois que l’agent a déterminé qu’une demande d’antidate sous-entendue a été faite, il détermine si une décision sur l’antidate sous-entendue peut être rendue au Niveau 1 selon la Politique nationale sur les niveaux de décision . Si le problème ne relève pas du Niveau 1, l’agent réassigne la question au Niveau 2. Politique nationale sur les niveaux de décision

Quand un AT Évaluation de la demande (EVD) ou Demande spécialisée (DS) est reçu, l’agent doit effectuer le calcul initial de la demande. Quand un AT Révision de la demande (RVD) avec un problème lié au nouveau calcul est reçu, l’agent doit effectuer le nouveau calcul d’une demande qui était finalisée. On se sert parfois de « recalcul » pour parler d’un nouveau calcul. Une fois qu’un calcul initial est bien transmis, un nouveau calcul d’une demande peut être effectué quand de nouveaux renseignements reçus auront une incidence sur le résultat du calcul précédent (p. ex. un RE modifié est émis). Quand un nouveau calcul est requis pour un cas d’Intégrité, un AT Action à prendre (AP) urgent est créé pour le nouveau calcul. L’agent assigné à cet AT doit effectuer le nouveau calcul. Le nouveau calcul d’une demande peut avoir une incidence sur : la possibilité du client d’établir une période de prestations (PP); période de prestations l’admissibilité du client aux prestations; le taux de prestations du client. Remarque

Quand l’enregistrement d’une demande crée automatiquement un AT RVD, dans SNCT, le champ Genre de prestations de l’AT RVD est prérempli par Régulier. L’agent met manuellement à jour ce champ avec le GP approprié. Pour une demande initiale ou renouvelée, l’agent choisit le GP indiqué dans la demande d’AE. Pour une demande de conversion dans une demande continue ou toute autre demande de conversion, l’agent choisit le nouveau GP demandé. Lors de la création d’un AT AP, Rappel (RA), Évaluation pour le calcul (ECAL) ou À revoir (AR), l’agent choisi le GP indiqué dans la demande d’AE. Si le GP a été modifié depuis que le client a présenté sa demande de prestations, l’agent choisit le GP indiqué dans ETI.

Peu importe la façon dont un agent organise son travail, l’agent à qui est assigné le calcul de la demande doit s’assurer que tout problème est résolu et que tous les faits nécessaires pour calculer la demande sont au dossier avant de compléter le calcul. À moins que les procédures fassent état d’une directive contraire, le calcul ne doit pas être complété tant que tous les AT nécessaires pour finaliser le calcul n’ont pas été complétés. Si le calcul ne peut pas être complété parce qu’il y a un AT connexe en suspens, l’AT du calcul doit être déplacé vers En suspens jusqu’à ce que l’AT connexe soit complété. Il se peut que des AT liés à une même demande faisant l’objet d’une évaluation soient assignés à divers agents (p. ex. un AT RE Litigieux motif de cessation d’emploi [MCE] est assigné à un agent et un AT EVD est assigné à un autre agent). L’agent complète seulement l’AT qui lui est assigné, sauf si une procédure prévoit le contraire. Lorsqu’il évalue une demande, l’agent à qui a été assigné un AT du calcul doit aussi examiner la Note client afin de déterminer les actions à prendre (p. ex. saisir des transactions, envoyer des lettres). Lorsque le calcul est complété, l’agent doit communiquer la décision au client si nécessaire.

Les parents peuvent partager les prestations parentales. Pour plus de renseignements et des définitions, l’agent peut consulter Parents : Définition — Tableau . Parents : Définition — Tableau Le genre de prestations parentales demandé par le premier parent qui a présenté une demande de prestations détermine le genre de prestations parentales auquel tous les parents sont admissibles pour la même naissance, adoption ou placement, quel que soit le parent qui est payé en premier. Lors du recueil de faits auprès des parents qui ont présenté une demande de prestations après le premier parent, l’agent informe les autres parents du genre de prestations auquel ils ont droit. Une fois qu’au moins une semaine de prestations parentales a été versée à l’un des parents, tous les parents demandant des prestations pour la même naissance, adoption ou placement ne sont admissibles qu’au genre de prestations parentales choisi par le premier parent qui a présenté une demande de prestations. Le maximum de prestations parentales standards partageables est de 40 semaines ou de 69 semaines pour les prestations parentales prolongées pour un enfant né ou placé en adoption le 17 mars 2019 ou après. Pour les enfants nés ou placés en adoption avant cette date, le maximum des prestations parentales standards partageables est de 35 semaines ou de 61 semaines pour les prestations parentales prolongées. L’admissibilité maximale des demandes de prestations standards pour un client demeure à 35 semaines ou à 61 semaines pour les prestations prolongées. Les clients peuvent modifier le nombre de semaines que chaque parent reçoit à tout moment avant que toutes les prestations ne soient versées. Quand les clients ne peuvent pas s’entendre sur le nombre de semaines que chacun recevra, l’agent réassigne la question à un agent de Niveau 2 qui rend une décision sur la division des semaines restantes. Remarque Une fois que la demande est établie et que l’admissibilité aux prestations parentales est déterminée, des prestations de parentales sont payables pour chaque semaine pour laquelle le client soumet une déclaration du prestataire et pendant laquelle le client : déclare 5 jours de non-disponibilité a fourni la preuve requise pour des prestations de parentales n’a pas reçu de rémunération ou de répartition empêchant le versement d’un paiement n’a pas fait l’objet d’une inadmissibilité empêchant le paiement Remarque

Quand le membre de la famille gravement malade décède, la période d’admissibilité aux PDC et la FC sont raccourcies et se terminent le samedi de la semaine au cours de laquelle le patient décède. Les PDC sont toujours payables jusqu’à la fin de la semaine au cours de laquelle le patient décède, peu importe le jour de la semaine (du dimanche au samedi) au cours duquel le décès a eu lieu. Rendre une décision sur la dernière période d’emploi dans la période de référence (PR) — DPP entre la s/c 2310 et la s/c 2361 Le budget 2021 a introduit une mesure de simplification temporaire à partir du 26 septembre 2021. Pour les demandes dont le DPP est entre la s/c 2310 et la s/c 2361, l’agent rend une décision sur la dernière période d’emploi dans la PR seulement si elle est litigieuse. Si l’agent autorise le dernier MCE, tout autre RE dans la PR, même s’il est litigieux, est utilisé pour calculer la demande. Cependant, si l’agent n’autorise pas le MCE du dernier RE dans la PR, la demande est calculée avec une exclusion. Remarque Cette nouvelle mesure ne s’applique pas aux demandes pour travailleurs indépendants et de pêcheur. Si le client qui demande des prestations pour travailleurs indépendants ou de pêcheur a un DPP dans la s/c 2310 ou après, un emploi assurable dans la PR et des RE litigieux, une décision doit être rendue sur ces RE selon les procédures habituelles. Quand le client déclare un MCE litigieux auprès d’autres employeurs dans la même demande, si TAD n’autorise pas le litige en vertu des règles de décision automatique, le litige est automatiquement résolu et TAD crée un rapport de décision (RD) qui indique Aucune décision requise . Le champ Condition spéciale du RE n’est pas mis à jour, et le RE est inclus dans le calcul. Aucun AT DEC n’est créé pour le MCE. Quand il y a plus d’un RE avec le même dernier jour payé (DJP), et qu’une des RE est litigieux alors que l’autre RE ne l’est pas, une décision n’est pas requise et les 2 RE seront inclus dans le calcul. Décision non requise : Motif de cessation d’emploi (MCE) au-delà de 12 semaines — DPP entre la s/c 2258 et la s/c 2309 Les principes de décision dans les demandes initiales ou de nouveau calcul dont le DPP est entre la s/c 2258 et la s/c 2309 s’appliquent seulement au MCE du dernier emploi dans la PR et aux questions liées aux MCE litigieux qui sont dans la période de 12 semaines avant l’arrêt de rémunération (A de R) utilisé pour établir la demande. Décision non requise antérieurement — Processus spécialisé du TAD Un nouveau processus spécialisé qui simplifie le traitement des demandes initiales a été présenté le 27 septembre 2020. Les demandes traitées dans ce processus spécialisé du TAD ont été établies sans rendre de décision sur les questions litigieuses liées au MCE dans la PR. Il est possible de repérer les questions liées au MCE pour lesquels aucune décision n’a été rendue, car le champ Condition spéciale a été laissé vide sur le RE, mais le RE a tout de même été inclus dans le calcul initial. Remarque Si aucune décision n’a été rendue sur un MCE litigieux dans la PR dans une demande initiale de prestations régulières lors du processus spécialisé du TAD, il n’est pas nécessaire de rendre une décision sur la demande renouvelée tant que le client demande toujours des prestations régulières. Cependant, il pourrait y avoir un AT DEC en suspens. S’il existe un AT DEC en suspens pour un MCE litigieux dans la PR, l’agent ne rend pas de décision sur la question. Pour supprimer l’AT DEC en suspens, l’agent envoie une demande à un utilisateur autorisé afin qu’il le supprime. S’il existe un AT EVD Renouvellement et un AT DEC en suspens pour un MCE litigieux dans la PR, l’agent de Niveau 1 traite l’AT EVD Renouvellement même si l’AT DEC demeure en suspens. L’agent : détermine la date d’entrée en vigueur du renouvellement; saisit le renouvellement et complète le numéro d’enregistrement; complète l’AT EVD Renouvellement. L’agent complète l’AT EVD Renouvellement avant d’envoyer une demande à un utilisateur autorisé afin qu’il supprime l’AT DEC en suspens. Remarque

Une mesure du budget 2021 s’applique aux indemnités de cessation d’emploi examinées entre le 26 septembre 2021 (s/c 2310) et le 24 septembre 2022 (s/c 2361) et versées en raison d’une mise à pied temporaire ou d’une cessation d’emploi permanente. Quand les indemnités de cessation d’emploi sont examinées pendant cette période, elles ne sont pas considérées comme une rémunération et ne sont pas réparties, peu importe le DPP. Les indemnités de cessation d’emploi non réparties ne peuvent pas prolonger une période de prestations (PP). Cette mesure s’applique à tous les genres de prestations (GP) pour les demandes initiales, renouvelées et continues et aux sommes suivantes, si elles sont versées en raison d’une cessation d’emploi : paie de vacances paie tenant lieu de préavis indemnité de départ allocations de retraite et crédits de congé de retraite crédits de congé de maladie primes de fermeture primes de fin d’emploi et de retraite sommes versées à la suite d’un règlement S’il est évident que les sommes sont des indemnités de cessation d’emploi, aucun recueil de faits n’est requis. Toutefois, il est toujours nécessaire d’effectuer un recueil de faits et de bien saisir les renseignements dans le RE pour les sommes comme les primes, les crédits de congé de maladie, les sommes versées à la suite d’un règlement et les indemnités pour retrait préventif. Si les sommes sont versées en raison de la cessation d’emploi, l’agent laisse les champs du RE indiquant une date vides et CAC ne répartit pas les sommes. Si les sommes sont versées pour toute autre raison, l’agent saisit les dates appropriées dans le RE et CAC répartit les montants comme d’habitude. Une paie de vacances versée lors d’une cessation d’emploi n’est pas répartie. Toute autre paie de vacances (p. ex. une paie de vacances incluse dans chaque paie ou versée à une date précise chaque année) est répartie selon les procédures habituelles. Fin de la mesure temporaire La mesure temporaire du budget 2021 selon laquelle les indemnités de cessation d’emploi n’étaient plus considérées comme une rémunération prend fin le 24 septembre 2022 (s/c 2361). À compter du 25 septembre 2022 (s/c 2362), les indemnités de cessation d’emploi sont de nouveau considérées comme une rémunération et une disposition temporaire s’applique pour s’assurer que les clients ne sont pas pénalisés par un examen tardif. Les nouvelles répartitions dont la date de début de la répartition est le 25 septembre 2022 (s/c 2362) ou après s’appliquent aux demandes initiales, renouvelées et continues et pourraient prolonger la PP, au besoin. Modifier une répartition existante Lors de la modification d’une répartition existante, les règles qui s’appliquaient à cette demande lors de la saisie initiale de la répartition s’appliquent toujours. Disposition temporaire À compter du 25 septembre 2022 (s/c 2362), lors de l’examen des indemnités de cessation d’emploi, si la date de début de la répartition est entre le 26 septembre 2021 (s/c 2310) et le 24 septembre 2022 (s/c 2361), les sommes payées ou payables en raison d’une mise à pied temporaire ou d’une cessation d’emploi permanente ne sont pas considérées comme une rémunération et ne sont pas réparties. La date de début de la répartition est la date à laquelle la répartition commencerait, même si aucune PP n’était établie pour cette période. Pour plus de renseignements, l’agent consulte Note de service AP 2022-04 — Retrait des mesures temporaires du budget 2021 : Soutenir les Canadiens et les entreprises jusqu’à la relance . Une mesure provisoire en vertu du Projet pilote 24 s’applique aux indemnités de cessation d’emploi versées en raison d’une cessation d’emploi dans les demandes dont le DPP ou la date de début de la répartition est entre le 30 mars 2025 (s/c 2493) et le 10 octobre 2026 (s/c 2572 ). Quand des indemnités de cessation d’emploi sont versées pour cette période, elles ne sont pas réparties. Des indemnités de cessation d’emploi qui ne sont pas réparties ne peuvent pas prolonger la période de prestations (PP). Cette mesure s’applique à tous les genres de prestations (GP) pour les demandes initiales, renouvelées et continues. Cette mesure s’applique aux genres de sommes suivantes, si elles sont versées en raison d’une cessation d’emploi : paie de vacances paie tenant lieu de préavis indemnité de départ allocations de retraite et crédits de congé de retraite crédits de congé de maladie primes de fermeture primes de fin d’emploi et de retraite sommes versées à la suite d’un règlement Pour qu’une demande soit considérée en vertu des mesures provisoires, elle doit remplir au moins une des 2 conditions suivantes : Le DPP est entre le 30 mars 2025 (s/c 2493) et le 10 octobre 2026 (s/c 2572 ). Les indemnités de cessation d’emploi seraient par ailleurs réparties en vertu des paragraphes 36(9) à 36(11) du RAE et la première semaine de répartition tombe dans la période commençant du 30 mars 2025 (s/c 2493) au 10 octobre 2026 (s/c 2572 ). 36(9) 36(11) Si aucune des 2 conditions n’est remplie, l’agent répartit les indemnités de cessation d’emploi selon les procédures habituelles de Rémunération . Pour plus de renseignements, y compris des exemples, l’agent consulte la Note de service AP 2025-05 . Rémunération Note de service AP 2025-05

Un étudiant étranger à temps plein qui étudie dans un programme et qui a un permis d’études valide comprenant une condition qui l’autorise à travailler n’a pas besoin d’un permis de travail pour travailler pendant ses études. Si l’étudiant travaille sur le campus, il n’y a aucune restriction quant au nombre d’heures qu’il peut travailler. Un étudiant qui travaille en dehors du campus peut, à compter du 8 novembre 2024, travailler jusqu’à 24 heures par semaine tout en fréquentant l’école et à temps plein durant les congés scolaires. Il n’y a pas de restrictions pour un étudiant qui travaille à la fois sur le campus et en dehors du campus, à condition que l’étudiant ne dépasse pas la limite d’heures pour le travail en dehors du campus pendant les trimestres d’études. Si l’étudiant travaille plus de 24 heures par semaine en dehors du campus pendant les trimestres d’études, une décision sur l’assurabilité est requise. Remarque

Un ressortissant étranger dont le permis de travail postdiplôme expire entre le 20 septembre 2021 et le 31 décembre 2023 peut travailler au Canada pour une période de 18 mois supplémentaires ou jusqu’à l’expiration de son passeport, selon ce qui se produit en premier. Les détenteurs de permis de travail postdiplôme admissibles ont reçu un courriel en août 2022 d’Immigration, Réfugiés et Citoyenneté Canada (IRCC) leur accordant une autorisation de travail provisoire jusqu’au 31 mai 2023. Si le permis a expiré entre le 20 septembre 2021 et le 1er octobre 2022, une preuve que le client a présenté une demande de renouvellement du permis de travail avant le 31 décembre 2022 est requise. Si le permis a expiré entre le 2 octobre 2022 et le 31 décembre 2022 et que le client avait un passeport et une adresse valides au dossier d’IRCC, aucune demande n’est requise et un nouveau permis de travail a été émis automatiquement au client. Si le permis a expiré entre le 2 octobre 2022 et le 31 décembre 2022 et que le client n’ avait pas de passeport valide ou d’adresse valide au dossier d’IRCC, une preuve que le client a présenté une demande de renouvellement du permis de travail est requise. Les détenteurs de permis de travail postdiplôme admissibles ont reçu un courriel d’IRCC en avril 2023, leur accordant une autorisation de travail provisoire jusqu’au 31 mai 2024. Ces clients sont considérés comme ayant un statut conservé aux fins d’AE : Si le permis a expiré entre le 20 septembre 2021 et le 31 décembre 2023, une preuve que le client s’est inscrit dans le cadre du processus simplifié (avant le 21 mai 2023) ou une preuve que le client a présenté une demande entre le 6 avril 2023 et le 31 décembre 2023 pour le renouvellement du permis de travail est requise. Remarque Pour obtenir un statut conservé, le client doit fournir les documents suivants : une copie du permis de travail; une copie du courriel d’autorisation de travail provisoire d’IRCC; l’un des documents suivants, selon la situation du client : une preuve de demande de nouveau permis de travail ou de renouvellement; une preuve d’inscription au moyen du processus simplifié; une déclaration du client selon laquelle il n’était pas tenu de présenter une demande (passeport et adresse valides); un nouveau permis de travail. Si le permis de travail du client expire avant la réception du courriel d’IRCC, le client doit fournir une preuve de son autorisation de rester au Canada au moyen d’un permis de visiteur, d’un permis d’études ou d’un autre permis de travail.

Une mesure du budget 2021 s’applique aux indemnités de cessation d’emploi examinées entre le 26 septembre 2021 (s/c 2310) et le 24 septembre 2022 (s/c 2361) et versées en raison d’une mise à pied temporaire ou d’une cessation d’emploi permanente. Quand les indemnités de cessation d’emploi sont examinées pendant cette période, elles ne sont pas considérées comme une rémunération et ne sont pas réparties, peu importe le DPP. Les indemnités de cessation d’emploi non réparties ne peuvent pas prolonger une PP. Cette mesure s’applique à tous les genres de prestations (GP) pour les demandes initiales, renouvelées et continues. Fin de la mesure temporaire La mesure temporaire du budget 2021 selon laquelle les indemnités de cessation d’emploi n’étaient plus considérées comme une rémunération prend fin le 24 septembre 2022 (s/c 2361). À compter du 25 septembre 2022 (s/c 2362), les indemnités de cessation d’emploi sont de nouveau considérées comme une rémunération et une disposition temporaire s’applique pour s’assurer que les clients ne sont pas pénalisés par un examen tardif. Les nouvelles répartitions dont la date de début de la répartition est le 25 septembre 2022 (s/c 2362) ou après s’appliquent aux demandes initiales, renouvelées et continues et pourraient prolonger la PP, au besoin. Disposition temporaire À compter du 25 septembre 2022 (s/c 2362), lors de l’examen des indemnités de cessation d’emploi, si la date de début de la répartition est entre le 26 septembre 2021 (s/c 2310) et le 24 septembre 2022 (s/c 2361), les sommes payées ou payables en raison d’une mise à pied temporaire ou d’une cessation d’emploi permanente ne sont pas considérées comme une rémunération et ne sont pas réparties. La date de début de la répartition est la date à laquelle la répartition commencerait, même si aucune PP n’était établie pour cette période. Un conflit collectif désigne tout conflit, entre employeurs et employés ou entre employés. Un conflit collectif peut être lié à l’emploi ou au non-emploi, ou aux conditions d'emploi. Peu importe si le conflit collectif a été initié par une grève ou par un lock-out, l’incidence sur la demande demeure la même. Quand un client perd son emploi ou n’est plus en mesure de retourner au travail en raison d’un arrêt de travail causé par un conflit collectif à son lieu de travail, il n’est pas admissible aux prestations d’AE en vertu de la LAE. L’agent de Niveau 1 peut traiter la décision, rendue par le coordonnateur régional, d’imposer une inadmissibilité ou d’accorder des prestations à un client qui perd son emploi en raison d’un arrêt de travail sur son lieu de travail si toutes les conditions suivantes sont remplies : La décision est tout à fait évidente. Aucun autre recueil de faits n’est nécessaire. Selon le recueil de faits relatif à la décision, on sait clairement à qui s’applique la décision. Si un agent de Niveau 1 ne peut pas appliquer la décision rendue par le coordonnateur régional, l’agent transmet le MCE au Niveau 2 pour qu’une décision soit rendue. Si le client présente une demande de prestations spéciales ou participe à la formation en vertu de l’Article 25, l’agent réassigne l’AT à un agent de Niveau 2 pour qu’il rende une décision.

Une décision sur le congé autorisé n’ est pas requise si l’emploi n’est pas assurable, car soit le client est embauché en vertu d’un contrat de service (travailleur indépendant), soit le client détient plus de 40 % des actions de l’entreprise. Si les faits au dossier indiquent clairement que l’emploi n’est pas assurable pour l’une de ces raisons, l’AT DEC ne doit pas être complété. L’agent suit les Procédures et conditions pour retirer les demandes du processus du TAD . L’agent déplace l’AT DEC vers En suspens jusqu’à ce que l’AT Évaluation de la demande (EVD) ou l’AT Demande spécialisée (DS) soit créé. Un utilisateur autorisé doit ensuite supprimer l’AT DEC.
